Catuṣpīṭhamaṇḍalopāyikā – Draft Edition –
Péter-Dániel Szántó, Balliol College, Oxford. 1v: Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Vajraḍāka!
Having first prostrated to Nāgārjuna, preceded by the four syllables,
I pay homage to the Buddha’s word— the secret that is utterly unmanifest—
through these secret instructions concerning the honey-cluster of the lotus.
I bow to the primordial dharma of the reality of gnosis (*jñānatattva*) when it is thoroughly purified;
I bow to the speech of the two [deities] of the nectar-taste of honey, which are the mud of the moon of the *ali*-gnosis belonging to the one with a vajra-mind.
He indeed perceives the ego within anger as knowledge in every respect;
by means of the Tilaka of the Path, through these three statements, I bow to that which is supreme for those traveling on the vessel, the lineage beyond birth and non-birth.
I bow to the Buddha’s word for the sake of deceased beings;
having seen the eighteen hundred thousand [verses] of the supreme Yoga-tantras, which are the secret pinnacle, I consider other treatises to be mere branches.
The speech of those driven by desire and discursive thought lacks the defining characteristics of the Word;
for all those who possess knowledge, the Yoga-sūtras and the entire Yoga-śāstra are like a theatrical stage for births that are as fleeting as bubbles in a dream.

Indeed, by this [statement], the words "delusion-delusion" proceed as the essence of the essence; having observed the pure path of Dharma and having taken hold of the pure Dharma, there is no doubt regarding the pure body.
But by Nīlaka, who was borne upon the chariot of non-duality,

the essence of reality was attained; through the vehicle of the cycle of existence, he conquered all that is to be conquered, and thus the lineage of instruction for this scripture was established, dedicated to the training of disciples.
The secret meaning has been concealed and expressed in the language of the Mlecchas;
twelve thousand [verses] in extent is the *Catuḥpīṭha-tantra*,
wherein the ritual for the mandala is revealed for one who has attained the application of reality.
And with eighteen divisions, one performs the play and embodiment of saṃsāra, as well as pacification, nourishment, subjugation, attraction, expulsion, paralysis, and so forth;
this is the mandala characterized by its targets, belonging to the fire-offering for the accomplishment of mantras and other rites.

By a good disciple, however, having drawn the mandala for the teacher who is supremely intent on the secrets of yoga and who is well-disciplined and discerning regarding reality— this is the first procedure for the examination and initiation of the disciple.
First of all, the preceptor should cause [the disciple] to perform the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) and so forth; having sat comfortably upon a seat in a location pleasing to the mind,
he should contemplate the sun in the palm of his hand, with the first vowel in its center.
On the left [hand], one should place [the fingers] adorned with the syllable of nectar situated in the center of the moon:
Śvetā, Dhūmā, Śaṅkhā, Padmā, Krodhā, and so forth on the right fingers; and Rocanā, Trimalā, Bhaṅgā, and Bhūcchannā on the left.
Jñāna and vijñāna are the two thumbs; in the ritual sequence beginning with the hands, Śvetā is for threatening and paralyzing, Dhūmā for piercing and causing immobility,
and Padmā for attracting all and charming by incitement.
Rocanā is the destroyer of the wicked; Trimalā is indeed the slayer.
It is renowned as the lineage of Māra, covered by the earth, and the performer of all rites.
For one joined with the application of gnosis, it is the consciousness joined with the left.

Having joined the right hand in the *kamalāvarta* gesture and the left hand in the hollowed-cup (*saṃpuṭa*) gesture according to the command of Śaṅkha, with the remaining fingers raised like needles, this is known as the *ali-mudrā*; its application is performed with the eight seed-syllables.
The tip of the vajra, blazing with light, should be visualized as the seed-syllable of fire for the upper [parts];
the eye of the earth; the space for the ears and nose;
and the eight nectars, white in every respect, as the seed-syllables of water for the tongue and the faculty of Indra (the eyes).
One should take the third of the eighth group, the fourth of that same [group], the first of the seventh, and the final letter of the eighth;
all of this, joined with the fifth of the sixth [group] and multiplied by three.
In the fourth [syllable] of the one descended from Repha (Ra) is Vāyu;
the four [syllables] of the crescent moon and bindu (Uṃ), together with six letters, are "Ambumoha" (Am-bu-mo-ha). [This is formed] by the neck, the earth, and the chest-pains.
One should place the syllables in their arrangement upon the heart-winds, the fire, the navel, and likewise the sacrificial animal, using the seed-syllables that have the forms of the deities,
situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala and contemplated as Vajrasattva.
Seated upon a lotus throne, with a radiance like that of snow or the kunda flower,
two-armed, in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, and crowned by the five Buddhas;
he holds a vajra in his right hand and places a bell at his left hip.
With all ornaments on his body and beautifully adorned with splendid garments,
one should recite and chant the mantra of Vajrasattva, who possesses manifold flames of light;
first, however, one should practice the seed-syllable of gnosis for three hundred thousand times.
One should bow to the final [syllable] joined with *bindu* and *nāda*, offered as a libation;
it is fit to be practiced by means of eighty-four thousand [recitations],
and twenty thousand [recitations] of *indrāmiḍī* should be chanted.

The worldly [deities] of the external seat are Rājendrī; they are accomplished by three thousand recitations of the *caṇḍikā* mantra. All [deities] are accomplished through prior service (*pūrvasevā*), but those belonging to the maṇḍala are not accomplished without such service.
Through the application of that mantra, the sequence of possession arises; this is the first [stage]. The second is the ritual for the preliminary service and the propitiation of the deity.
In that regard, those intent on the propitiation of mantras quickly cause the entry [of power] into both stationary and moving beings as prescribed by the mantra:
Oṃ vajrāveśaḥ.
If one wishes to cause the Buddha to enter [into oneself], one should perform three hundred thousand recitations with the mantra *oṃ hili 2 hūṃ jaḥ*.
Through three hundred thousand recitations, the entry by sight of humans and others is accomplished.
Oṃ mātali hūṃ phaṭ. Through three hundred thousand recitations, success is attained; the world shall experience the descent of the *śruta* (hearing).
Oṃ mātali, you who move the mind, hūṃ [phuṃ] phaṭ.
The yogi should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times to effect the remote possession of humans and others;
the practitioner of the mantra should recite "Oṃ vatuli 2 hūṃ phaṭ" three hundred thousand times to perform the preliminary service and other rites.
For one who has become a *nāga*, the entry of all deities into the secret place and so forth occurs;
the yogi should recite "Oṃ pātini pātini hūṃ phaṭ" one hundred thousand times to perform the preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*) and other rites.

The master should cause water, clods of earth, stones, and trees to be entered [into the mandala] first; thereafter, for those who are disciplined and well-discerning, he should teach the reality of the mandala and so forth, being intent upon the preliminary service and other requirements.
For those who have not propitiated the deities and who are a mockery to themselves,
one should meditate [on the victim] as being possessed by Vajrasattva and others, with vajra and bell in his two hands, situated upon the foremost wind-maṇḍala.
In the heart, the winds of the winds are set in motion by the wind-seed syllable;
then, the wisdom-vajra at the tip of the vajra is moved within the heart. Following that movement, one assumes the form of a lioness and utters a forceful *hūṃ* with a threatening gesture.
By means of the previously mentioned mantra-yoga, one should destroy [obstacles] with water containing flowers and so forth;
for the superior, middling, and inferior [practitioners], O man, one should specifically cause [the deity] to enter:
*hūṃ rama rama ho ho ho a a aḥ phaṭ*.
If one who has been entered by doubt regarding the consecration of the reality of yoga should [seek] the immersion into this yoga of mantra and so forth, then at that very moment,
there will be immersion into the reality by these beings known as humans; of this there is no doubt.
However, for this reason, one must examine those who are unworthy among those possessing superior knowledge.
Now I shall describe the great medicine: by bringing the gods under control, even those who are unworthy may surpass other humans due to the abundance of their previous merit.
By means of this mantra-incense, there is an immediate possession;
having then made [the victim] a goat, one should recite the five-limbed secret yoga of the yogins with the fire and wind elements according to their respective locations.
In the heart of the seed of knowledge, joined with seven fires,
one should prepare equal parts of great guggulu oil; this guggulu, combined with the seven great medicinal herbs, is like the water of immortality.
One should fumigate and worship at the proper time, and having recited the Vajra-seed mantra, one should smell its fragrance; then, even at that very moment,
the Kṣedikās and Dyotikās, joined with the five hooks, will become possessed.
One should cause the five substances beginning with *unmatta* to be made in equal parts, mixed with *mahātaila* and combined with *amṛtodaka*; by that,
one is possessed of the sense of taste of the tongue at that very moment.
The teacher, having written the mandala, should constantly teach the Dharma to a disciple who is well-discerning and possesses the application of a superior being,
while [the disciple] stands before the Three Jewels with a body and so forth that are pure by nature.
He was sweet-spoken and dear to all, his mind governed by compassion;
he was devoted to the study and recitation of the scriptures, delighted in giving, and was pure through his dedication to the Mahāyāna and the secret Dharma.
"Constant and perpetual devotion to the Guru—this is the gathering of that disciple.
Thus ends the third procedure, the examination of disciples for total immersion (*sarvāveśa*).

Now I shall explain the procedure for the mandala, which accomplishes all attainments: first, with a mind established in compassion, one should perform the consecration of the ground in a pleasing location, avoiding any impure places.
Having prepared the pure ground and so forth, the wise one should there construct the mandala,
adorned in various places with canopies spread above, divine hangings of many kinds of cloth, banners, parasols, and bells.
On the first day of the fortnight and so forth, having first performed the collection of the ritual site,
one should smear it all around with scented water and, using powders of white, yellow, and other colors, place an eight-petaled lotus at the four corners.
Having placed the vase in the center according to its name as the "all-action" [vase],
one should first arrange the five-colored thread upon the petals; then,
having established the vajra in the south, one should place the bell in the north.
One should serve the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in a conch shell at the western petal; the powder of the colored dust (rajacūrṇa) is applied to all sides of the lotus.
Having donned the armor of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), one [visualizes] oneself as Vajraḍākinī.
For one engaged in this worship, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, and bali offerings, the characteristic of seizing the ground is as follows:
having formed two vajra-fists, one places them upon the tips of the breasts.

Having pervaded everywhere with your entire being, descend upon the ground; let whoever may be there— lords of the site, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, gandharvas, bhūtas, bhūtanis, and ḍākinīs— all depart from this place.

"O you who have begun the work for the benefit of sentient beings, go forth immediately! Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra and mudrā for dispelling obstacles. Having formed two vajra-fists, one should hold the two joints together. "Oṃ, grant your favor, O Mother; you are beautiful, as requested by me. Oṃ hūṃ jruṃ jruṃ svāhā.
This is the mantra and mudrā for requesting the ground. Then follows the characteristic of the resonance of the vajra-bell, which will be described below.
Holding the vajra and the bell, he should maintain perfect concentration;
he should visualize the goddess Vajraḍākinī seated upon a lotus throne within the flask, having brought her to completion with a full form and radiant beauty.
One should worship the divine one of white complexion and radiance, holding a pair of vajras and bells in his hands,
with all things and noble offerings combined;
having formed both fists, he holds up white *arocana*.

Having formed the *kuñcika* (key) mudrā with the tips of two fingers, one should display the mudrā at the heart; *oṃ aḥ svāhā* is the mantra for the heart-mudrā. One should touch the tip of the *vajra* to the water-pot (*kumbha*) and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.

With the seed-syllables of the five Buddhas, one should sprinkle the five threads and so forth; *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. With the seed-syllable of Siṃhinī, *kūṭa*, one should sprinkle all the colored powders (*rajas*); *oṃ smryuṃ svāhā*. Then, in that place, for the yogins, preceded by the offering of the *daityā-bali*, [one should proceed].
One should cause the offering of food-oblations to be given in the eight locations of the Lord according to the mantra of the former, for the purpose of securing the ground; furthermore,
the artisan, through his work, should cause the training in the observance of the pledge to be performed.
Having withdrawn everything by means of all [mantras], one should again smear the vases on the right side with perfume and then have the lines for the mandala drawn;
this is the fourth procedure, the ritual for the acquisition of the site.
The preceptor, having carefully determined the specific layout of the lines,
should color the five [circles] with nine fresh colors using five pigments; [he should do this] for the central points of their respective grounds by means of the eight directional positions.
Having observed that there is no deficiency in any of the locations,
the wise one should sustain all of them with the syllable *hūṃ*;
this is the self-manifestation of the application of Vajrasattva.
One should have two [disciples] with joined palms perform the ritual preparation of the thread;
the sprinkling-thread (*prokṣasūtra*) should be consecrated with the mantra consisting of the seed-syllables of the five ḍākinīs: *oṃ a ā ā āṃ svāhā*.
This is the mantra for sprinkling the thread. Having taken the hand of the guru, one [should place] a single disciple nearby.
Having established the disciple in the northeast and the guru in the southwest;
or alternatively, the disciple in the southeast and the guru in the northwest;
with the disciple in the eastern position and the guru in the western positions.
The disciple [should enter] from the north side, while the teacher [enters] from the south; it is adorned with eight directions and subsequently beautified by a square,
complete in every respect in the center of the vajra-maṇḍala.
In the fifth [section], one part out of three is for the innermost [area];
the ends are surrounded by the outer positions of the yoginīs starting from the edge; the central maṇḍala consists of nine squares and is adorned with vajra-pillars.
One should arrange four *viśvavajras* in the interior corners; the door of the five-part [mandala] is likewise [divided], as are the chest and the half-chest,
excluding the archway (*toraṇa*) from the one-part [section].
One should cause the doors and the altar for the deities to be made on one-fourth [of the area];
the door should be one-eighth part, and one should cause all the lines of the altar to be made with colored powders.
For the nine-square section of the inner sanctum, one should use powders of the colors of the directions.
The exterior of the site, however, should be [marked] with red powder;
one should cause five walls to be provided for that outermost area and the rest of the site, which is adorned according to the nature of the ground.
One should arrange the deities and other elements in a place that is entirely like molten gold,
square-shaped, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
beautified by vajra-pillars, and embellished with various ornaments.
Well-adorned with garlands of networks of small bells, necklaces, half-necklaces, and so forth, and decorated at its four corners upon a moon-disc with a vajra,
one should raise a banner at the door, which has two water-pots and a garland.
The lion-emblem of the lotus is raised in the eastern direction;
the peacock and lotus emblems are designated for the northern direction;
and the banner and swan are the positions for the lotus in the western direction.
One should also join the eighth direction, the south, of the lotus marked with a *makara*,
which is endowed with straight vajras and so forth, in its respective place; by these means, one attains the state of being the abode of all Buddhas through the reality (*tattva*) of the mandala.
From the *kalaśa* as well, one should place eight [vessels] in the eight directions;
having filled them with scented water and adorned them with the tips of sprouts, one should arrange four at the sides of the doors and the others elsewhere.
One should draw Jayamaṅgala in the east, Siddhi and Ṛddhi in the north, Vijayakalaśa in the west, and Siddhighora in the south,
starting from one cubit up to sixteen cubits in size.
For yogins who desire peace, prosperity, or subjugation, the mandala of the eastern section is determined by the preceptor;

thus ends the fifth chapter: the ritual for the preparation of the knowledge-thread, the colored powders, and the placement of the vases. Then—[one should visualize] one's own body as the deity, fashioned from Vajraḍākinī.
O Master, if disciples should arise at the four gates and it is impossible to manage them all, one should apply the two mantras as prescribed for a single purpose;
first, by means of the practice of casting [the spell], one should dispel the wicked Māra.
Brandishing the vajra toward the sun and sounding the bell toward the moon,
having cast it four times, one should direct the gaze toward the east and other directions with the mudrās; [this is performed] with the feet level, the feet apart, and the left side bound together.

The Vajra goddess should recite "Haṃ," followed by the terrible utterance of "Hūṃ" and "Hūṃ": "Oṃ Hūṃ! Strike! Slay the wicked! Destroy them! Aḥ Aḥ Hūṃ Hrīḥ Phaṭ! At the northern gate, having filled the air with the sound of the syllable "Hūṃ" resonating from the vajra-bell, she should recite "Haṃ," O Ghorī, while manifesting [the rite]; her two hands joined and pressed against the region of the heart.

Having manifested the form of Vettālī through the *ālīḍha*, *pratyālīḍha*, *vaiśākha*, and *maṇḍalapada* stances, [uttering] *oṃ hūṃ 3 āḥ phaṭ*, one should cast her toward the western direction. Holding the two signs at the hip joint with the hands,
and having placed the feet touching the knees, one should cast the weapon and, having rotated it, [assume] the posture of being trampled by all lions (*sarvasiṃhākrāntaka*).
Filling [the space] with the sound of *hūṃ*, one should utter *oṃ hūṃ āḥ phaṭ*;
having manifested the form of Cāṇḍālī, one should place her upon the head of the one whose hands are joined at the right door.

Having uttered the seed-syllables of the knee-step, the dog-step, the clockwise-turning step, and the counter-clockwise-turning step— the fierce and terrible *hūṃ*— one who is intent upon that [should recite]:
*oṃ hūṃ āṃ phaṭ*.
Even in the previous location, one should again perform the shifting of the place;
having placed Vajrapāṇi at the heart, one should place the bell on the left hip.
One should establish the pride of self as Jñānaḍākinī, with the syllable *HŪṂ* residing therein.

Restrained in the *ālīḍha* posture, the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and the *ālīḍha-saṃyata*, and restrained in the *pratyālīḍha-saṃyata*, he should then slay those who obstruct enlightenment in the center. With his body protected by armor consisting of a fence of spiked enclosures, his self being the union with the Jñāna-Ḍākinī, and seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, having joined his two hands in a hollowed cup and extended them so that the tips touch, [he recites]: OṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ.
The mantra of the cage-seal (*pañjara-mudrā*): Having firmly bound the "clinging-bond" (*lagnabandha*), one should raise up wisdom and realization (*jñāna-vijñāna*).
One should then encircle the eight directions with the earth-umbrella, lotus, and needle. *Oṃ jambhani hūṃ phaṭ*.
This is the mantra of the great enclosure seal (*mahāprākāra-mudrā*). With the hands joined in the upward-facing gesture, a vajra is visualized right there.
At the location of the five *āsphānas*, there is the purification of the seven netherworlds (*pātālas*). Thus, with the heart-triangle *kīla-mudrā*, the mantra is:
*oṃ juṃ phu phaṭ*.
This is the sixth procedure, the protection of the maṇḍala. Then—the practitioner, seated comfortably, [should visualize himself as] identical with Vajraḍākinī.
Those who have compassion for all sentient beings should also sprinkle [water] from the vase.
The vase is said to be fourteen-fold; it is the characteristic of that which has been taught as reality.
Having filled the water-jar with water drawn from the Mandākinī, one should recite the *mandākinī* mantra seven times—mixed with the mantra: *oṃ tapte mahātapte hūṃ svāhā*.
Having well-mixed various fragrant flowers with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and having adorned them all with sprouts from the branches, one should offer the seats;
they are covered with cloth for the necks and beautifully decorated with an abundance of splendor.

To cause the jar to be offered with garlands and strings of flowers mixed with milk, one should perform the "earth-umbrella" finger-knowledge gesture; having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should kiss the remaining [portion] raised upward and touch the jar on all sides:
OṂ HŪṂ SUṂ KṢUṂ YUṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ.

The mantra for the mudrā of holding the vessel is: *m-aṣṭasya*. Then one should establish its name. Thereafter, the body of the Preceptor, consisting of the essence of Yogāmbara and endowed with a self-nature, should be adorned with a great stage-curtain cloth or the like, beautified by eyes and other features, with all ornaments on the limbs, and with the five Buddhas as a crest-jewel.
Having donned the armor of the factors of awakening with a well-composed mind,
one should bestow the cuirass upon him and perform the binding of protection;
having extended both hands, they should be encircled by knowledge and discernment.
Having formed the shape of a swan’s wing and rotated it within the heart, [one recites]:
*oṃ hūṃ pheṃ phaṭ*. This is the mantra of the Great Armor Mudrā (*mahākavacamudrā*); may it protect that which is being protected, held as it is with vajras and bells.
Having grasped the two as reality, one should recite "I am Vajrasattva" with the *tripatāka* mudrā; his vajra is raised,
and the eight-syllable mantra is to be meditated upon in its entirety with the eight limbs.
The tongue is water, and this space belongs to the ears and nose;
earth and this sky are to be joined with fire and the blazing of Brahman;
[the senses] have moved from the necks of the charioteer Mōha and are situated in the heart.

One should indicate the deities of this [body] by means of the eight limbs of the conceptualization located at the heart, the head, the two eyes, the two ears, the mouth, the two nostrils, the navel, and the root of the genitals;
one should perform self-worship with flowers, incense, lamps, and fragrance.
Oṃ vajrakāya hoḥ;
oṃ vajravākya aḥ;
oṃ vajrahṛdaya hūṃ.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure; I am vajra-pure.
Oṃ, all phenomena are yoga-pure; I am yoga-pure.
"Ahamvajra" means "the pinnacle of the stages of awakening of the Vajra";

this is the seventh procedure for performing the yoga of the self. Then—having commenced the Mahāyoga—one [should worship] all the deities of the yoginīs by means of the Meru arisen from existence (*bhava*), following the sequence of mantra and mudrā.
The seed-syllable of Vajrī is joined for the purpose of satisfying Anila and Anala; having ascended through Bindu and Nāda, which pervade the four elements,
and having first joined them for the sake of satisfaction, it becomes like another ocean of milk.

The peak of the seed-syllable is preceded by *vajra*, belonging to all the Lords; it is the lion-throne for the primordial wisdom of the *Ādibuddha* and others within the maṇḍala of all yoginīs, adorned with a sun-maṇḍala,
and the *ālikāli* [vowels and consonants] are situated within the center of the seed-syllable in a specific form.
He has three faces and six arms, with a splendor surpassing that of a dense rain-cloud;
he has three eyes, is smiling yet wrathful, and is colored by the aesthetic sentiment of passion (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Seated upon a living being in the paryaṅka posture, he is closely joined in union with the body of Prajñā.

The arrangement of arrows is upward; with two [hands] he grasps the *liṅga* and breast, while with the third he holds a thunderbolt. On the left, however, one should place an upward-pointing bow; and the left [hand] is marked by two [vessels] completely filled with nectar-water.
Adorned with beautiful garments and ornaments by the third [deity] Ghaṇṭānāda, his matted hair is bound with a silk band, and his skull-crown is formidable;
he is adorned with all ornaments by the symbols of the sixth.
One should place the sky-like yoga of the Buddhas, possessing manifold rays and flames;
the weapon, white in color and most beautiful, is the seat for that Prajñā.
Furthermore, the linga of the neck is grasped by the two with a sharp edge at the door.
Having encircled the joint with one foot, let him dissolve into the Vajrapadma;
with a mind focused on the center, he should meditate upon this Buddha in union with his consort, whose limbs are adorned with all ornaments and beautifully decorated with garments.
The lords of the nāgas placed their playful seat, which was born from the syllable of nectar, with its graceful posture; [the deity] who has the luster of a white kunda flower,
possesses two arms, has disheveled hair, and is adorned by the five Buddhas.
Her body was adorned with snake ornaments; she had three eyes and uttered the wrathful syllable *hūṃ*.
She held a *khaṭvāṅga* staff and a yogic bowl, from which issued manifold rays of blazing light.
She wore an elephant hide as her lower garment and was draped in human skin.
Vajraḍākinī, adorned with a circle of fire, is situated in the east; she is brilliantly beautiful, yellow in color, possessing a weapon, laughing an eightfold laugh,
terrifying, blazing, with hair standing erect, and crowned with the five Buddhas.
Seated upon a peacock throne in the half-lotus posture,
his body adorned with all ornaments, he shines with two arms and stands within a circle of fire, holding a khaṭvāṅga staff and a yogic vessel.

One should visualize the terrible Ḍākinī on the northern side of Jñāna, seated upon a Garuḍa-throne in the utkaṭāsana posture, wearing an elephant hide as a lower garment and covered with a human skin.
She is of beautiful red complexion, two-armed, and utters a terrible *hūṃ*.
Her hair is blazing and disheveled; she is adorned by the five Buddhas and decorated with ornaments of snakes, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a yogic bowl.
Clad in an elephant hide and covered with a human skin,
one should meditate upon the Western Goddess as Bindu and Nāda in the East;
she is blue in color, the most terrible Mahāghorī, the eight-laughing Bhairavī.
Seated upon a servant’s seat, standing with his feet in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture,
with disheveled hair streaming out, adorned by the five Buddhas,
two-armed, laughing with a loud roar, and possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire.
Adorned with ornaments of snakes,
she wears a garment of elephant hide covered by human skin;
having ascended the *nāda* and *bindu*, Caṇḍālī is the Mistress of the South.
White and yellow in color, standing in the *lalitākṣepa* posture,
with a divine radiance like a flame of fire, two-armed, making the wrathful *hūṃ* sound,
and beautifully adorned with red-colored ornaments of snakes.
Above the sword, with the left hand holding the noose of the index finger,
one should perform the visualization of the seed-syllable placement for Dahanī, the enemy of all Māras;
this involves the projection of the mandala of white, black, and other colors as her seat.
One should meditate on her as having two arms, laughing with wrath, and clothed in red garments; she holds a seed-syllable of a radiance equal to the flames of fire,
and displays the goad, the noose, and the threatening gesture (tarjanī) that cuts through all the wicked.
He is resplendent with a red and black complexion, adorned with two arms, holding a battle-axe, a noose, and a threatening gesture; he is clothed in red garments,
seated in the half-lotus posture, and adorned with a circle of fire.
According to the seed-syllable, however, in the east is Aṭṭahāsī; Bhairavī is seated upon a jackal,
positioned in the utkaṭāsana posture,
holding a staff, a threatening gesture, and a noose, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Clad in red garments, having meditated upon the arrangement of the seed-syllables, she sits upon a seat of emission; from the eastern gate comes the Ḍākinī,
white in color, with great blazing flames, adorned with disheveled hair.
With his hand placed in his mouth, adorned with serpent ornaments,
wearing red garments, and mounted upon a chariot created by the syllable *phuṃ*,
he sits upon his seat while Dīpinī stands to his north.
The great Ghorī of yellow complexion has her hands joined in *añjali* placed upon her head;
she is born from the syllable *pheṃ*, seated upon a corpse-throne beautifully adorned with red garments, while Cūṣiṇī is situated to the west.
Clad in red garments and possessing great radiance, she should drink the blood held in her joined palms;
generated by the syllable *Phraṃ*, she guards the western gate,
seated upon her entire throne, while Kambojī stands to her right.

Black in color, with great flames, and clothed in red garments, he is born from the syllable *Phrīṃ*; holding yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and a mouse, he is encircled by three garlands of vajras; he is considered the refuge for those devoid of fear.
On the external circular pedestal, seated upon a lotus and moon throne, are Oṃ Ha Hoḥ Hrīḥ;
Pukkasī, Ḍrāmiḍī, Caṇḍī, and Saubhāgī, with their hands busy [holding implements]. To the north are Ghrīghra, Ghorī, Rucirā, and Māṃsī, holding five goads and full vessels.

In the west, Padmabhāṇḍapibānī, with hands busily occupied, is Jvalitā Bībhatsī; in the south, Balipragāḍhapaṅkajapāṇinī, is Vartulī Hūṃ 3 Kapālī Vajrī Kumbhī; with hands busily occupied by various kinds of food and drink, in the northeast is Hūṃ Lāsya, possessing erotic grace (śṛṅgāra), while Vāma is proud;
Hūṃ Supriya Mahāśaṅkha, with perfumes, mudrās, and ointments, in the southeast is Hūṃ Ho, playing the lute (vīṇā) with the vajra-mudrā.

With hands joined in a hollowed cup (*saṃpuṭāñjali*) and holding flowers, one should cast half of them toward the southwest while uttering "HŪṂ" three times; raising a white [flower], one should cause it to resound.

With "IṂ" and incense, one should fumigate with a flickering glance and the moon of the junction. In the northwest, with dance and "HŪṂ" syllables, one should be in the triple-bent posture (*tribhaṅga*), proud on the left.

With "KṢUṂ," with hands joined in a hollowed cup for the lamp, and through the yoga of the salutation-gesture (*praṇāmāñjali*): these twenty are to be worshipped according to the distinctions of the common families and colors.
"One should arrange those outside the vajra-fence according to their beauty"—
thus ends the eighth [chapter], the procedure for the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the deities of the supreme seats (pīṭha) of supramundane gnosis.
Having placed Kheṣahaṃ in the eastern direction— blue in color, four-armed,
seated upon the throne of Garuḍa, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
and fashioned as the doorkeeper bearing the discus, sword, mace, and conch.
On his right side, one should place Lakṣmī, adorned with a yellow crown; she holds a lotus in her right hand. To his left, however, is Vārāhī, produced from the syllable *vaṃ*.
O Boar-faced one, [you who are] wrathful, with a skull-ornamented crown and fierce,
dark-blue complexion and great flames, wearing yellow garments; [you hold] your beloved on the left, a red skull-cup in the left [hand], and a smeared-off head in the right.
At the northern gate is the Oṃkāra of Brahmā, resembling blood-red in color,
four-armed and four-faced, adorned with a crown and beautiful form,
seated upon a swan-throne, and holding the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and a garland of *akṣa* berries.
In his left hands, he holds a lotus, a water-pot, and a chowrie, while his right hands are raised;
on his left side is Brahmāṇī, equal in appearance to her own lord, marked with the syllable *vaṃ*,
and on his left [side] is Sarasvatī, marked with the syllable *saṃ* and possessing the luster of emerald.

At the western gate is one whose body is adorned with a heavy garland of flowers, intent upon playing the lute; he is white in color, seated upon a bull, wears a tiger-skin garment, bears the crescent moon on his crown, and has the *turāsanga* (the mark of Viṣṇu) on his chest. *Hūṃ saṃhara*.
He has three eyes, holds the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), and a trident (*śūla*) in his hands;
he is solely intent upon singing and dancing to the resonance of auspicious sounds. To his left, however, through the syllables *māṃ*, there is the equality of sovereignty with Māheśvarī.
However, [he should be visualized] with a rosary in his right hand, while on his left is the Gaṅgā, formed by the syllable *gaṃ*; she is equal to her own lord,
holding a lotus and displaying the gesture of granting boons— a goddess worshipped even by the gods of the thirty-three heavens.
At the southern gate is Śakra, white in color and greatly radiant;
in his middle hand he draws a vajra toward his heart, while his left hand rests gracefully upon his hip,
his hands busy holding a jewel parasol, and he is adorned with a jeweled crown.
On his right side is Indrāṇī, born from the *iṃ* syllable,
equal to the sovereign everywhere, with a skull and tawny hair tied upward;
on the left is Tilottamā, born from the *tiṃ* syllable, golden-brown in color.
Holding a goad in his right hand and a slender creeper-staff in his left,
wearing a golden crown like a Jambū tree, with all his limbs adorned with ornaments, he stands in the northeast in the royal posture of Indra.
He holds a vajra drawn to his right heart and rests it playfully upon his left lap;
seated upon the throne of Airāvata, he is ever intent on worship. To his right, Śacī, with her attendants, possesses a splendor equal to her own lord.
In his right hand he holds a three-pronged vajra, and with his left hand he draws toward his heart the maiden Karpitayaṣṭikā;
she has arisen from his left side, possesses the luster of emerald,
and her hair is adorned with mandārava flowers and mirrors.
In the southeast, at the tip of the wealth-treasure, is Kuvera, wearing a jewel-crown,
beautiful with a golden-yellow complexion;
he holds a seed-vessel in his right hand and a creeper-tree in his left, seated upon a vetāla throne.
To his left, however, are the Vasumatīs, golden-hued, with syllables of the sound "vaṃ";
they adorn his body which is graced by all ornaments and shines with two arms; on his left is Mañjī, who holds grain and bestows fearlessness with her right hand.
To his left, by means of the syllable *phaṭ*, is Hārītī, resembling an emerald,
her body adorned with all ornaments, holding the Varada mudrā and an Aśoka flower;
and in the southwest is the King of Spirits (*bhūtarāja*), black in color and seated upon a horse.

Wearing a crown of skulls, he holds a staff in his right hand and displays the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in his left; he is honored with a jewel-crown. To his right side is Laṅkeśvarī, born from the syllable *laṃ*.
He has a skull [crown] with hair standing upright, is green with the luster of emerald,
holds the best of weapons in the right hand and a red skull-cup in the left;
to his left is the Yoginī Raṃ, who is fond of the color red.
With a red complexion and a great blaze of light, his emblem is identical to that of the Lord of Laṅkā;
in the northwest, Varuṇa is fashioned from the syllables *bhūḥ* and *bhuvaḥ*,
seated upon a crocodile throne, white and red with a great blazing radiance.
He holds a boon-granting noose and is adorned with a jewel crown; on his right side is Bhogavatī, resembling a young coral sprout, marked with the syllable *Bhauṃ*,
and bearing a crest of peacock feathers and holding a fly-whisk in her right hand.
To the left of the one whose body is being torn apart, there is the gazing at the breast; from the left arises a swan, a practitioner fond of the blue lotus,
white in color, with great radiance, and adorned with a crest-jewel upon its hooded leaf-like head.
She holds a blue lotus in her right hand, and her left knee is marked with a wheel;
she is encircled by a garland of vajras upon the seat of the worldly deities.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the procedure for the colors, arms, and mounts of the worldly deities on the Yoga-seat.

Having established [the deities] starting from the eastern direction within the twenty squares of the heroic [mandala] on the outer circular pedestal, one should place Karaṅkabhairava at the syllable *kaṃ* and Kamalākarī upon his lap.
On his right, however, one should place the syllable *khaṃ* for Khaṭvāṅga-rākṣasa;
likewise, for Maṅka, one should establish the syllable *khaṃ*, and on his left, one should place the syllable *gaṃ*, which has a deep resonance, for the goddess Kharanakhrī.
Seated upon his lap is the Goddess, sounding deeply with the syllable *gaṃ*;
at the center of the upper wheel is the syllable *ghaṃ*, which is Ghaṇṭākarṇaka;
seated upon his thighs is the Goddess Ghaṃkāraghaṭasunī.
On its southern side, one should place Caṇḍeśvara with the syllable *caṃ*; the Goddess Capalānanī embraces him. To his left, however, one should place Cchidraghoṇa with the syllables *cchiṃ*.
Mounted upon his lap is the syllable *chiṃ*, which has gaps between its teeth;
in the western cell of the pedestal is the syllable *jaṃ*, dear to those born from a womb;
seated upon his lap is the syllable *ja*, which strikes down the wicked.

In its left chamber is the sound *jhaṃkāra*, terrifying with its *jhaṃkāra*; the Goddess embraces it, she who makes the sound of love with her *jhaṃkāra*. In its right-hand chamber is the sound *ṭiṃkāra*, the syllable *ṭiṭṭibha*.
Mounted upon his lap is Ṭikkāra, adorned with Ṭikka ornaments;
in the middle right cell is Ṭhīkāra, whose body is the color of glowing embers;
seated upon one of those is Ṭhaṃkāra, together with the beloved Ṭhakkā.
On his left side, one should place the syllable *ḍaṃ*, the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and the *ḍaṃvara*; seated upon his lap is she who is fond of the *ḍiṇḍima* drum, [represented] by the syllable *ḍiṃ*.
In the second left square, with the syllable *ḍhaṃ*, is the tumultuous sound of the *ḍakkā* drum.
Raising her onto his lap with the sound *ḍha-kāra*, she who is fond of the *ḍhakka* drum;
in the chamber of Īśāna, with the sound *ḍha-kāra*, she who is dear to him; seated upon his body with the sound *taṃ-kāra*, she whose thighs are like those of an elephant.
In that second square is the syllable *thoṃ*, with a *thora* arm; he is seated upon its throne. In the syllable *thaṃ* is *Tharaṅginī*.
In the southeast corner of the square, in the syllable *daṃ*, is *Daṃṣṭrākarāla*.
Seated upon his lap was one with lips red as vermilion; in the second cell was one who uttered terrible cries of "dhik";
and mounted upon her were yoginīs who spoke with deep, grave voices.
In the south-western direction, in the second chamber, there is Piṇḍabharas, who sits upon his seat with the syllables *pīṃ*; he has tawny eyes due to the syllables *pī*.
In that second chamber, there is Phenamukha with the syllables *pheṃ*.
Seated upon his lap, the goddess, her eyes blossoming, utters the sound "pheṃ"; having placed the syllable "baṃ" in the northwest quadrant as the resonance of Brahman,
the yoginīs, relying upon that, [visualize] the syllable "baṃ" as the one with graceful limbs.
In that second chamber was Bhīkāra, who utters terrifying roars; upon his lap was mounted Bhramarakeśinī with her humming sounds,
and in that excellent city of celestial chariots, the entire assembly was surrounded by twenty heroes.
There were five crest-jewels, a garment, loose hair,
the lap of a yoginī, a lap-sash, a yoga-trident, and a vessel; indeed, there was various and manifold food as well as very pure drink.
"One should practice the yoga of the supreme seat of knowledge (*jñānaparapīṭha*), which consists of the five desires.

Thus ends the tenth [chapter], the ritual procedure for the non-dual worship of the heroes (*vīrādvayapūjāvidhi*) in the Secret Seat (*guhyapīṭha*). Having brought forth the circle of knowledge (*jñānamaṇḍala*) drawn from the wheel of commitment (*samayacakra*), and having established it within the wheel of commitment, [one establishes] the non-dual circle of knowledge.

Having placed before him a bathing vessel made of gold or another such material, filled with milk mixed with sesame seeds, parched grain, fragrant barley, and the scent of white flowers, he should also place within it a well-polished mirror.

Having formed two vajra-fists (*vajramuṣṭi*), encircled by the white earth-canopy (*bhūcchatrā*), this is known as the White Hook (*śvetāṅkuśā*), the supreme for summoning the commitments (*samaya*). With this hook-seal (*aṅkuśamudrā*): *oṃ vajrāṅkuśa jaḥ*. Having thus summoned the supramundane [deities], one should place the *rocanā* on the third joint of the left hand’s *trimalā*, which is raised above the *trimalā*; having bound the smoke-hook seal (*dhūmāṅkuśamudrā*) in this manner: *oṃ ākarṣaṇi hūṃ phaṭ*. Having thus invoked the mundane [deities] and firmly bound the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*), with the *trimalā* and smoke raised—

Having consecrated the water for the *argha* offering twenty-one times—either three times seven or twenty-one—with the mantra *oṃ pratīcchārghaṃ hūṃ svāhā* while holding the vessel, one should present the *argha*. Then, taking the *vajra-muṣṭi* mudrā, one should playfully cast a lotus, a conch, or incense smoke [into the vessel] joined with white collyrium. Taking a flower with this mudrā and consecrating it with the previously mentioned mantra *oṃ pravarasatkāraṃ pratīccha svāhā*, one should offer the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and worship with the five offerings and so forth, by means of the *hūṃkāra-antarikā*.
With an auspicious song, "Hūṃ 3," she is fashioned;

the Yoginī has created your entire body. You are the secret one, the binder of the twelve-fold [worlds], the one who has swallowed the Vajra and moved it upward. Brahmā is found there, Hari is the doorkeeper, Indra holds the parasol, and the assembly of Kinnaras and Ṛṣis sing auspicious songs.
[She is] one whose belly is large and whose lips hang down like the roots of a tree at the end of the rainy season.
Having established it upon a beautiful stand made of *sukacchra* wood,
it should be adorned with garlands of flowers produced from rivers, ponds, and the like, and its neck should be encircled by a wreath of flowers fastened with gold thread.

Having drawn [the deity] according to the samaya with the mantra "Oṃ tapte mahātapte," one should sprinkle [it] with water from the Mandākinī. Then, performing the knowledge of the "earth-umbrella" (bhūcchatra) finger-gesture, one should kiss [the deity] with the mudrā "The remainder is raised" (śeṣam ucchritam), while reciting "Oṃ suṃ kṣuṃ yuṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā" seven times and touching [it]. If possible, there should be various musical instruments such as drums, conchs, and flutes, accompanied by great joy.

At the time of the ritual bath for the resonance of the vajra-bell, one should first begin with an anointing using fragrant oil and *āmalaka* fruit. Then, with water mixed with fragrance, followed by honey;
thereafter, with milk and water from a conch shell, and then with fragrant flowers. Then, having formed two vajra-fists, one should hold them upright;

then, casting that same [mudrā] blue-colored [flower], one should place it above the head while reciting the mantra "Oṃ hūṃ svāhā. Having offered a garment, then, as before, one should offer the *argha*, *pādya*, and so forth, using the mantra and mudrā.

Having formed two vajra-fists and bound the noose-mudrā known as the "white yellow-oxide chain" (*śvetārocana-śṛṅkhalā*), one should cause [the disciples] to enter with the mantra *oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ*. Then, having firmly bound that same noose-mudrā as the "lioness" (*siṃhinī*), one should expel the obstructors while reciting with wrath the mantra *oṃ smryuṃ svāhā*. Next, having formed two vajra-fists joined back-to-back—the vajra-sphoṭa mudrā—one should secure the door with the mantra *oṃ vajrasphoṭa vaṃ*.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the ritual procedure for the invocation of the wheel of knowledge and the bath. Then, having formed the *samayamudrā* of the Tathāgatas and others with the mantra *oṃ tiṣṭhāsana hūṃ svāhā*, one should display the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*). There, having performed the turning of the lotus on both sides with the counter-mudrā (*pratimudrā*), there is the binding of all mudrās;
by means of the lotus-command, the ground-parasol (*bhūcchatra*) of the one who stands is pressed down by gnosis (*vijñāna*).

Having formed two chains and raised the remaining three banners, one holds the five-pronged vajra of the smoke of the three impurities (*trimalādhūma*). This is the *samayamudrā* of the Tathāgata Redyogāmbarī. The mantra is: *oṃ vajrasattva dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ samayas tvaṃ samayas tvaṃ m-aham*. At the end, there is also the heart-mantra of that deity: *trivaiṣāvrārya*. As for the mudrās: having firmly bound the *vajrabandha*, one raises the smoke of the three impurities with *oṃ hūṃ haḥ svāhā*.

The *arghamudrā* itself is the *samayamudrā* of the Prajñāpāramitā-Ḍākinīs; their mantras are: *oṃ aṃ aḥ svāhā*. Thus for Prajñāpāramitā. *oṃ hūṃ haḥ svāhā*. Thus for Jñāna-Ḍākinī. Placed upon the fourfold *vajrabandha* and empowered by primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), *oṃ suṃ saḥ svāhā*. Thus for Vajra-Ḍākinī. Having raised up primordial wisdom and consciousness, she herself is considered to be Ghorinī: *oṃ kṣuṃ kṣaḥ svāhā*.

Thus, for Ghorāḍākinī, the needle [is made] from a lotus, earth, and an umbrella; she herself is considered to be Vetālī: *oṃ yuṃ yaḥ svāhā*. Thus, for Vetālī, the needle [is made] from smoke, iron, and impurity; she herself is considered to be Caṇḍālikā: *oṃ huṃ haḥ svāhā*. Thus, for Caṇḍālī, the needle is a composition of a lotus, earth, and an umbrella, with white *arocana* as the stylus. This was taught by the Sage Samaya in the fourfold Lion’s Roar (*siṃhanādicatuṣṭaya*) for the Ḍākinīs and other gatekeepers situated within the circular maṇḍala. *Māhiya*.
The three mudrās themselves are the samaya-mudrās, while the mantras are designated as the kāmī-mudrās;
thus ends the twelfth chapter, the procedure for the supramundane samaya-mudrā mantras.

For others who are accompanied by their consorts, the mantra-mudrās are prescribed as follows: having raised the fist itself, the subsequent ones are known as the *samayas*. Oṃ khe saḥ svāhā. Having placed Hari’s own fist at the heart and moved it again and again, this is briefly declared by the Sugata to be the *samaya* of Brahmā: Oṃ oṃ svāhā. Having formed Brahmā’s “sun-fist” (*sūryamuṣṭi*) and cast it as a triple-bannered gesture (*tripaṭākika*), that is the supreme *samaya*-establishing mudrā of Śūlin: Oṃ hūṃ sha svāhā. Having firmly bound Rudra’s “moon-fist” (*candramuṣṭi*) over yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*sūrika*)...

Having extended [the hand] like a parasol toward the sun, one should place it down with: *oṃ ma su hūṃ svāhā*. Having touched Śakra’s [forehead], it is considered the *samaya* of Indra when placed obliquely on the forehead with: *oṃ sa mu hūṃ svāhā*. Having firmly bound Indra’s *vajrabandha* and joined the raised white *arocana* in the form of a jewel, one should show it to Kubera with: *oṃ dhanāgre hūṃ svāhā*. Having formed Kubera’s *sūryamuṣṭi*, the white [hand] is raised as a sprout.

The well-known pledge-seal (samaya-mudrā) of Bhūtādipa, as transmitted by the Sage, is: *oṃ khātani hūṃ phaṭ*. By that same [seal], having formed a fist, the white smoke- and sprout-arisen seal is proclaimed by the Jina as the pledge-seal of the Lord of Serpents (*phaṇināṃ pati*): *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā*. For the Lord of Nāgas and his wives, the pledge-seal is the very seal of their own lord; however, their mantras are specified as follows: *oṃ lakṣmyai svāhā*, *oṃ vārāhyai svāhā*.
Oṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī; Oṃ, svāhā to Brahmāṇī; Oṃ, svāhā to Māheśvarī.
Oṃ gaṅgāyai svāhā | Oṃ aindrāṇyai svāhā | Oṃ tilottamāyai svāhā ||
Oṃ, svāhā to Śacī; Oṃ, svāhā to Rambhā;
Oṃ, svāhā to Vasumatī.
Oṃ, svāhā to Hārītī; Oṃ, svāhā to Laṅkeśvarī; Oṃ, svāhā to Raktapriyā.
Oṃ bhogavatyai svāhā;
Oṃ utpalapriyāyai svāhā.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter: the ritual procedure for the samaya-mudrās and mantras of the deities of the yoga-pīṭha. Then, having formed the vajrāñjali, one should press the two forearms together.

Through the union of gnosis (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*), it is proclaimed in the Lotus Vessel (*padmabhāṇḍa*) that these are the *samayamudrā* mantras for Karaṅkabhairava and the others, as well as Kamalākārī and the others; furthermore, the mantras for their respective consorts are: OṂ KARAṄKABHAIRAVĀYA SVĀHĀ and OṂ KAMALĀKĀRĪYAI SVĀHĀ.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Khaṭvāṅga-rākṣasa! Oṃ, svāhā to Kharanakhī!
Oṃ, svāhā to Gambhīranāda!
Oṃ gambhīranādīyai svāhā; Oṃ ghaṇṭākarṇāya svāhā;
Oṃ ghaṭāstanīyai svāhā.
Oṃ caṇḍeśvarāya svāhā | Oṃ capalānanīyai svāhā | Oṃ chidraghoṇāya svāhā ||
Oṃ, svāhā to Chidradaśanīyā; Oṃ, svāhā to Jarāyudhapriya; Oṃ, svāhā to Jayanonnatī.
Oṃ jhaṃkārabhīmāya svāhā | Oṃ jhaṃkṛtakāñcīyai svāhā | Oṃ ṭiṭṭibharakṣāya svāhā ||
Oṃ ṭikkabhūṣaṇīyai svāhā.
Oṃ ṭhīvanoṅgarāya svāhā. Oṃ ṭhakkakāminyai svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to the one who possesses the hand-drum and the drum; Oṃ, svāhā to her who is fond of the small drum;
Oṃ, svāhā to the tumultuous sound of the large drum.
Oṃ ḍhakkalālasīyai svāhā; Oṃ taṅkapriyāya svāhā;
Oṃ tanujaṅghīyai svāhā.
Oṃ thorabāhave svāhā. Oṃ tharaṅginīyai svāhā. Oṃ daṃṣṭrākarālāya svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to Darasminī! Oṃ, svāhā to Dhikkāraghora!
Oṃ, svāhā to Dhīrabhrāṣiṇī!
Oṃ, svāhā to Piṇḍacara! Oṃ, svāhā to Piṅgalākṣī! Oṃ, svāhā to Phenumukha!
Oṃ phallanayanīyai svāhā; oṃ brahmadhvanāya svāhā;
oṃ bandhuragātrīyai svāhā.
Oṃ bhīmanādāya svāhā;

oṃ bhramarakeśīyai svāhā. Thus ends the fourteenth [chapter], the ritual procedure for the mantra of the Samaya-mudrā of the Non-dual Hero at the Guhya-pīṭha. Having sealed it there with the four mudrās as before, beginning with the tongue and so forth.
The first vowel-syllable is the tongue; you are the Dharma-mudrā in every respect. Performing the turning of the lotus, one should employ the Vajra-sphoṭa.

Having drawn it forth as it moves within the heart, one should place the arrow at the edge of the ear. Thus is the Karma-mudrā of the Tathāgata Yogāmbarī. Embracing her breast with one's own arms, the wise one should press it; *Oṃ śriyatame hūṃ svāhā*.

Having encased the moon and sun within the Jñānaḍākinī, one should cause the lotus-form to blossom; for Prajñāpāramitā, the consciousness is placed upon the ground-umbrella, while the remaining [deities] arise as Vajriṇīs. (14) For Vajraḍākinī, her gnosis should indeed be joined with lotuses; for the eastern [direction], she is joined by being touched; for Ghorāḍākinī, having formed a *añjali* with both hands and placed it at the mouth, one should cause it to blossom;
for Vetālī, having firmly formed a vajra-fist, white *arocana* arises.

Having joined it with the form of the jewel, the adept should display it to Caṇḍālī; he should perform the double vajra-bind of Caṇḍālī, [reciting] "Oṃ smryuṃ svāhā," which is the chain of white *arocana*. For Siṃhinī, having firmly bound that same mudrā, [he should visualize] the smoke rising from the three impurities.

Oṃ ymryuṃ svāhā. Having joined that very same mudrā of the tigress, [one performs] the chain of the earth-umbrella and the eyelashes: Oṃ hmryuṃ svāhā. For the jackal, having firmly bound the vajra-fist, there is the supreme thrice-snap: Oṃ kṣmryuṃ svāhā. For the owl, laughing, one casts the sun and moon into her mouth: Oṃ phraṃ phraṃ svāhā. For the ḍākinī, having placed the añjali at the crown of the head: Oṃ pheṃ phraṃ svāhā.

For Dīpinī, one should cast the *preta-añjali* mudrā into the mouth: *oṃ pheṃ phaṃ svāhā*. For Cūṣinī, having firmly bound the *candramuṣṭi* mudrā, one should hold it at the root of the ear: *oṃ phreṃ phraṃ svāhā*. For Kāmbojī, one should extend the *candra-hasta* mudrā, joined with the knowledge of the *bhaṅga*.

Having established the *sūryahasta* (sun-hand) mudrā, the [mudrās] of Pokkasādi and others are proclaimed: *oṃ hā hā hrīḥ svāhā*. Having extended the *candrasūrya* (moon-sun) mudrā of Pokkasādi and others, one should form a hollowed enclosure (*saṃpuṭa*) above it: *oṃ ghriṃ ghraḥ svāhā*. For Ghorī and the others, having firmly formed the *vajrāñjali* (diamond-clasp), one should tear asunder the sun and moon: *oṃ kuru kuru svāhā*. For Ugrī and the others, having first extended the *candrasūrya* [mudrā], one should join back with back.

One should restrain the fingers of the hands by means of the chain-binding (*śṛṅkhalābandha*): *oṃ vatuli hūṃ svāhā*. Having formed the two vajra-fists of Kapālī and the others, one should hold them at the junction of the hips; by bowing with a trembling of the heart, this becomes the commitment (*samaya*) of Lāsyā: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. For Lāsyā, having extended the moon-hand (*candrahasta*), joined with the knowledge of the bend, and grasping it with the sun-hand (*sūryahasta*), it is proclaimed as the scent-conch (*gandhasaṃkha*): *oṃ supriyagandhe hūṃ svāhā*. For Gandhā, the scissors (*kartarī*) are held at the heart-moon, raised up and elevated upon the staff of the arms.
Raising the instrument toward the sun with the mudrā called Kaṭākā: *oṃ hūṃ hoḥ svāhā*. For the lute (*vīṇā*), having formed a hollow like the sun and moon, one should contract it and cast it upward;

by means of the application of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), this becomes the commitment (*samaya*) of Puṣpā: *oṃ sriṃ svāhā*. For Puṣpā, having raised a white [flower] from the fist while it is moved by the sound of *hūṃ hūṃ* and flickered before the mouth, this is considered the commitment of Gītā: *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*. For Gītā, having firmly bound the vajra-fist, it is grasped at the joint by the moon.

By means of the ritual application for offering incense, the mudrā of Dhūpā is declared as: *oṃ iṃ svāhā*. One should place the hand of Candrapāṇi on the right hip of Dhūpā; having raised the hand of Sūryapāṇi, one should hold it above her head: *oṃ sunṛtye hūṃ svāhā*. Having placed the añjali of Nṛtyā at the crown of the head through the application of the añjali of salutation, the Dīpa-mudrā is proclaimed for the bending of the body to the left: *oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā*. For Dīpā, having extended [the fingers] toward the solar portion, one should unite them with white [light] through gnosis (*jñāna*).

That which arises is proclaimed as the Moon Seal (candramudrā); its mantra is *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. When applied with the moon, the Vajra Seal (vajramudrā) is sung of as the Bell Seal (ghaṇṭāmudrā); its mantra is *oṃ ho svāhā*. Having joined the moon and sun together, one should apply them to the secret place; having moved the lotus-like parasol, it is proclaimed as the Dhyāni Seal (dhyalimudrā); its mantra is *oṃ aḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the seals of all ḍākinīs. By means of gnosis, one should tread upon the lotus; the remainder is the needle that pierces the life-force.

The mantra of the *astra* (weapon) is renowned in the maṇḍala of the Yoginīs: *oṃ tīkṣṇe svāhā*. This is the mantra of the *astramudrā*. Furthermore, in the application of the moon (*candraprayoga*), the Sugata has likewise taught that the *apāstra* (non-weapon) mudrā exists in the maṇḍala of the Yoginījāla: *oṃ ghūrṇita hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the mantra of the *apāstramudrā*. For all those possessing both the *astra* and *apāstra*, [the procedure is as follows]. Moreover, the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) itself, when devoid of specific symbols, is the Action Mudrā (*karmamudrā*). The mantras, however, are those previously specified.

Furthermore, the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) for all these mundane and supramundane [deities] is by means of their own previously mentioned mantras. The form endowed with its own insignia, ornaments, garments, colors, and gestures is indeed the great seal. Having thus sealed them with the four seals as before, preceded by the calculation of the eight limbs, one should perform the empowerment of the blessing of the three bodies and the armor. Then, having offered satisfaction, the water for the feet, and the guest-water with the hanging silk banner and the gesture of equanimity, and having worshipped them thoroughly with flowers and other offerings—

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Ritual of the Four Mudrās of the Mundane and Supramundane Deities. Thereafter, preceded by the turning of the lotus: in the form of *ālāsya*, in the form of a lute (*vīṇā*), in the form of a flute (*vaṃśa*), in the form of a *phaṣa* [musical instrument], in the form of a small drum (*paṇava*), in the form of a fan (*vyajana*), in the form of a banner (*dhvaja*), in the form of a canopy (*vitāna*), in the form of a flag (*patākā*), in the form of an umbrella (*chattra*), in the form of musical instruments, in the form of a girdle (*mauñjī*), in the form of a kettle-drum (*paṭaha*), in the form of dancing, in the form of laughing, in the form of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), in the form of wrath, and in the form of drawing an arrow from a quiver.

Having performed worship with twenty mudrās—by means of the *vāja-lālanā*, by the gesture of the joined palms (*añjali*), by the song of the syllable *hūṃ*, and by the various fruits such as the *śrīpāla* and others which bestow manifold results—one should join the sun and moon to form the *saṃpuṭa* fruit-gesture. The mantra for this fruit-gesture is: *oṃ jrūṃ svāhā*. Thereafter, the wise practitioner should perform worship through the essential reality (*tattva*) of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

Having filled the vessel with the nectar, one who knows the divisions and is a knower of all principles (*sarvatattvavit*) should place the Sun and Lotus upon the seat and sprinkle the *cumbaka* with "Bhaṅgavijñe. With "Oṃ ha ho hrīḥ svāhā," one should perform the churning of the deity three times.
Then, having filled the vessel with the *chidriṅga*, one who possesses everything should cause it to be offered in the eight locations of the eighth [deity].

One should cause the five [implements], such as the hook (aṅkuśa) and so forth, to be sprinkled according to their true nature and offered with everything and by everyone; likewise, various kinds of food and drink should be given. OṂ ŚRĪṂ HŪṂ GHUṂ HŪṂ A SVĀHĀ. This is the mantra of the five hooks. OṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ GHUṂ GHUṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ. OṂ GHEṂ GHEṂ PHEṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ. OṂ PHEṂ PHUṂ PHAṂ PHRAṂ PHEṂ PHUṂ SVĀHĀ. Having satisfied [the deities] with this sixteen-syllable mantra of satisfaction, the knower of reality (tattvavid) should then sound the vajra-bell and brandish the vajra, saying: "Sohia vajja ullālu tāria satu vimokkhu. (O Vajra, lift up! Cross over! This is the liberation!)
In the *Dharmavimokṣa*, it is said: "One should avoid the faults of action and maintain the purified shadow...

[as in CaPī III.1.34]. Thus, having brandished [the bell] according to reality and formed two diamond-fists joined back-to-back, one should move the "earth-umbrella" (*bhūcchatrā*) and the "lotus-encompassment" (*padmaveṣṭā*) with the syllable *HŪṂ*. *Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe hūṃ hoḥ | Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇitapraraṇite sarvabuddhapracālite | Prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajradharahṛdayāvatoṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ 3 a svāhā.*

Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe ... a svāhā. This is the mantra for the Vajra-bell mudrā (CaPī III.1.35–36). One should worship [the deity] with reality through the resonance of the vajra-bell, using white flowers and so forth, incense, rice, curd, and cooked rice;
and having worshipped in the northeast with molasses mixed with honey, thereafter—
Having offered white flowers and incense along with noble vessels of milk,
one should present various offerings to be worshipped in the northwestern direction, filling beautiful vessels with food such as rice equal to my own portion.
One should cause foods such as ground sesame cakes to be offered in the south-western direction; however,
the wise person should especially offer those prepared with delicious delicacies mixed with curd, honey, and ghee in the southeastern direction.

With sublime fragrances of flowers, sublime incense and lamps, and sublime offerings upon sublime sites, one should worship all [the deities]. Thus concludes the sixteenth procedure for the offering of bali in the four outer corners. Then, having accomplished the knowledge of equality, the preceptor, well-composed in meditation, [should proceed].
When the moon is present, there is the resonance of the bell; when the sun is present, there is the vajra-lalita. All these are to be honored, with faces smiling with passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
One should satisfy all the yoginīs by means of the form of the song of the syllable *hūṃ*.

Regarding the application of the logic of mudrās, one should observe the form of whichever mudrā one binds, provided it is equipped with a bow, an arrow, and a quiver; it should be beautified by the chanting of the syllable *hūṃ* and filled with auspicious sounds.
O Primordial Supreme Being, O Great Joy, O Great Delight— O Lord of Vajra-Arrogance, O Lord whose very self is Samantabhadra!
O supreme samādhi of the mind-being, Vajrasattva of great power;
foremost in the conduct of Samantabhadra, crusher of Māra and the forces of Māra;
all-enlightenment, great enlightenment, the Buddha born before all Buddhas, the foremost of the foremost.
Vajra-hūṃkāra, hūṃ-maker, Lord of the World, bestower of jewels,
great passion, great bliss, great wealth of desire and liberation,
[you who are] in the three times, in the three worlds, the foremost of the three, the supreme of the three realms, and of the triple world.
The most excellent among the immobile, manifest, extremely subtle, and the accumulation of the gross;
having attained the state of the most excellent among the mobile, he is the purifier of the cycle of existence (bhava-saṃsāra);
without beginning or end, primordial, beautiful, and established within all things.
O you who are the commitment of the yoga of the heart-mudrā; O great festival of the reality-being (*tattvasattva*);
O Vajra-anger, O great anger; O burner, O restrainer at the time of universal dissolution; O supreme subduer of the wicked; O Rudra, O fierce one, O terrifying one!
The Tathāgata of great accomplishment, the great roar of the activity of Dharma,
the path of excellent action of the True Dharma, the purifier of the mind of awakening, the great purity, the Great Lotus (Mahāpadma), the great wealth of wisdom and skillful means.

O Maheśvara, supreme in the samādhi of the purity of passion, O Universal Passion! O Infinite Space, eternal reality, great abode of all beings! O Manifestation, Lord of Fortune, King who fulfills all hopes!

Homage be to you! Homage be to you! Homage be to you! Homage, homage! With devotion I take refuge in you; O Vajrasattva, grant me success today! Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the ritual of praise beginning with "Supreme Purity. Then—by means of the offering of hymns accompanied by the resonant sound of the vajra-bell:

They sing the vajra-songs, considered to be various forms of *oṃ* and *hūṃ*: "Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O bearer of the body, the supreme saṃsāra! O Vajradhara, who holds the joy of embracing the consort! Hūṃ, you are that; hūṃ, you are that; hūṃ, you are that—O you whose excellent feet are worshipped by the best of gods! [O you] who are adorned with flowers and free from anger!"
O Vajra, you are my refuge! You are my refuge! You are my refuge! You are my refuge!
In the supreme state of liberation from conceptual existence, O secret one, take me as your own! Delight, delight! O Vajra, you are my refuge! You are my refuge! You are my refuge!
You are my refuge! You are my refuge! Press me to your secret place! You are my refuge! You are my refuge! You are my refuge! You are my refuge! You are my refuge!

O you who destroy immeasurable sin, you who are the destroyer of the seven accumulated [defilements], you who have transcended the worldly existence that is nourished by the enjoyment of sense-objects—*teṇṇā huṃ teṇṇā huṃ teṇṇā te te huṃ*. I bow to the former Lord, seated upon the crest of the noble king of elephants, whose body is adorned with a white conch and moon, who is immeasurable, and whose body is perfected in the five [senses]. Bow down to the one who is free from passion (*vajjia*).
O Lord, conquer! Your body possesses the most excellent golden luster; you are adorned with a beautiful necklace and decorated with young antelopes.
O Sovereign Goddess, your limbs are beautifully reddened by lotus-paste; you are filled with passion, your face marked with the *hūṃ* syllable, and you are terrifying with the sound *hūṃ*.
Ghaṇṭā, with a terrible staff and fearsome, is the Goddess in the west; she bows to the Lord and is adorned with blue.

She has a heart of malice, bears Hari, Hara, and Indra upon her head, and is the destroyer of Māra, possessing wrath. O Hūṃ-emitting Ḍākinī, bow down to me! This is the fifth song of the reality of the Vajra-bell, resounding with its resonance.

Singing their own unique [song], mixed with the fifth vowel (*ā*), they chant: *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*—the five Buddhas, the five *ḍākinīs*. Having created all the *ḍākinīs* from that very essence, in the void and the non-void, in the void of saṃsāra, having brought about existence and non-existence, give [it]!
To that very one, O *yoginī*, give the staff; excluding the others, give the *buddhayoginī*!
Having obtained the seven mandala-remedies, the King and Queen sang songs to the lute;
having avoided what is fit and unfit to eat, they performed worship.
Having abandoned the path of worldly attachment, they attained perfect nourishment through the five senses; by the service of the goad, they lived upon food fragments.
I behold the joined palms of Kālī; the essence of the True Dharma, the manifold expansion.
O Lion, look upon the Dharma and liberation! O Protector, O Protector, you are the true being!
Having exhausted the miserable cycle of existence, by your devotion, you have become a circle of light that delivers the world.
The lion has devoured the deer; the tiger has well burnt the wicked one.
Seeing everything whirling like a bat, look at the *pheṃphekkā* [sound]! O hero, bow down to that thunderbolt; you are the savior from this saṃsāra.

O hidden one, enjoy the immeasurable; with devotion, worship me as the great honey. Singing the songs of the yogis of reality, they describe the fifth state (*pañcama*) through the resonance of the vajra-bell, intent on various forms of worship. O Lord Supreme of the Sovereign of Reality, you whose crown is the play of the venerable [deity], and who are radiant with the beauty of the excellent seat of the venerable Guhya.

One should perform various offerings of hymns, songs, and praises, such as: "The reality of the yoga of the vibrating resonance of the glorious Vajraghaṇṭā; the supreme lord Śrījñānalābha, who enjoys the [divine] pleasures. Having formed the vajra-añjali mudrā and held it at the region of the heart, one should worship with the mantra: *oṃ śuddhadharme hūṃ aḥ āḥ āḥ āḥ svāhā*. This is the eighteenth procedure for the offering of songs on the supramundane reality. Thereafter, the external bali-offering should be performed by those of discernment.
It may be performed with the [actual] heroines when they are available, but if they are not available, it should be performed with [their] substitutes.
With a garment such as a great stage-cloth or one adorned with eyes and so forth,
his body [adorned] with all ornaments, holding a vajra and bell in his two hands,
and with a parasol in his hand— [this is] for Śakra; the second [is] fanned by Brahmā.
Hari is the doorkeeper of the foremost; Hara is proclaimed as his name;
Lalitākṣepapāda is the utterance of *hūṃ*; Pūrvadṛṣṭika is the resonance of the moon-bell; and Sūryavajra is cherished as the [sound] *vajra*.

One should cause a square fragrant mandala to be strewn with white flowers; for one endowed with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer a generous meal of śāli rice along with half-sugar and ghee as a drink, starting from the eastern gate.
Having formed two vajra-fists joined back-to-back, one should raise white *arocana* powder encircled by the earth-umbrella and lotus;
with the hands white and slightly curved, [one should address] the asuras, non-asuras, and siddhas: *oṃ vattali mahāvattali hūṃ 3 jaḥ svāhā*.

The mantra for the mudrā of drawing [the deity] through the eastern gate: Having perceived the vessel with Candra, and having raised the white Sūryavajramuṣṭi, [one should recite] in the *lalitākṣepa* posture: Oṃ vāhani mahāvāhani pretavāhani sūryacandrasiddhimukhi japarāji somarāji umādevī gaṅgāsvarūpi tārā saṃgraha sarvagaṇapati kārttika śrī śaśidevī agalo pagalo asurasurarāja pukkasi mahāpukkasi hūṃ he ho ākarṣaya 2 samayādhipatya hūṃ 2 phaṭ jaḥ.

Svāhā! Having satisfied [the deity] with the invocation mudrā and the mantra "Oṃ bhakṣa 2 samayādhipati jruṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," which is encircled by white *arocana*, one should dismiss [the deity] with the mudrā-mantra. This is the *devabali*.
Then, at the northern gate, standing with feet even, one should brandish the vajra while sounding the resonance of the vajra-bell as before.
For the purpose of the white maṇḍala, one should place vessels of milk and so forth; with white flowers and incense, an offering of milk-rice should be presented,
employing the previously mentioned mudrā and the mantra associated with it.

Having firmly formed the *candramuṣṭi* (moon-fist), having extended the knowledge of the terrestrial umbrella (*bhūcchatra*), and having joined the solar hand (*sūryapāṇi*) in the shape of a hood (*phaṇākāra*).

The binding of the vessel’s seal is to be performed by one who has undertaken the vow: *Oṃ Ananta, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Kuliśapāla, Devatī, Mahādevatī, Saumyaśikhi, Mahāśikhi, Daṇḍadhara, Mahādaṇḍadhara, Ayaṇāla, Huluṇḍa, Nanda and Upananda, Sāgara, Mahāsāgara, Tapta, Mahātapta, Śrīkānti, Mahākānti, Ratnakānti, Surūpa, Mahāsurūpa, Bhadrādika, Mahodara, Ṛṇṇi, Mahāṛṇṇi.*

Oṃ, come, come, O Lord of the Great Nāgas! Sarve bhūr bhuvaḥ phuṃ phaṭ svāhā! One should offer the northern *nāga*-bali and dismiss it with three snaps of the fingers. This is the *nāga*-bali. Having first invoked the Yakṣa-lord from the west by means of the mudrās and so forth, one should perform the ritual of casting the mandala while sounding the vajra-bell.

A red maṇḍala should be prepared with red, yellow, and other flowers, along with perfumes, flowers, and the like, especially the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). To the west of the Yakṣa-lord, who was previously invoked and established, [one should recite]: *Oṃ Māṇibhadra Pūrṇabhadra Subhadra Jayabhadra Nandikīla Mahākīla Mahīkīla Padmaśikha Śaṅkhaśikha Naha Mahānaha Bhedani Chedani Pūraṇi Dhanādhana Sudhana Surūpa Keli Mahākeli Hasita Krīḍita Vikṣepa Suśipra Svarūpakānti*.
O Vajreśvarī, by my command, O Yakṣa, O Yakṣiṇī, hūṃ! Descend, descend! Pattali, devour [her] among the beloved yoginīs, hūṃ 3 phruṃ svāhā!
Having firmly formed the "naked fist" (*nagnamuṣṭi*) mudrā and pressed it against the region of the heart—thus:

oṃ dhanādhipa pattali 2 phraṃ svāhā. One should give three snaps of the fingers as an offering (*bali*) to the yakṣas with all [the mantras] ending in *sarvaka*. Treading upon it with the vajra-foot, in the third [position], with three [steps] in the middle.
One should draw a triangular maṇḍala with a substance stained with blood,
accompanied by red flowers, incense, offerings of food, and vessels containing onions, blood, meat such as that of a cat, and the like.
One should offer the southern *bali* consisting of sesame flour, *kulmāṣa*, and especially the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), as well as various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten;
having first invoked [the deity] with the mudrās and mantras beginning with the eastern one, [one offers it] while standing to the south.
He struck the great-sounding drum with the *paṭaha* three times, saying:
"Oṃ! Whether at a single tree, in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a cave, or a grotto, by the side of a village, in a field, or especially in an empty house."
In a vessel placed upon the ground, one should especially worship Mātaṅga, as well as Kṛṣṇarudra, Mahārudra, Devadatta,
Kṛṣṇakāla, Bībhatsa, and Nandātīta Vināyaka.
Cāmuṇḍī, the terrible and loathsome Umādevī, who is the source of all; Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, and Sthūlakālī the Yoginī.
Indrī, Candrī, Ghorī, Duṣṭī, Lambhakī, Tṛdaśeśvarī,
Kāmbojī, Dīpiṇī, and Cūṣiṇī— the Yoginīs established in the villages,
who possess terrible forms, great forms, and hands made fearsome by their fangs.
Adorned with garlands of skull-bowls, possessing great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), holding khaṭvāṅgas, swords, and spears in their hands, as well as vajras, bows, and so forth—
O Mahāsukha, O Mahāvajra, you who accomplish all activities!

The Great King of the Yoga Maṇḍala, the Lord Vajrādhipati, the Tathāgata’s great body, the stainless creator of yoga—this is the Vajreśvarī mantra for all purposes: Oṃ ka kka [ka5] ḍṛṇa bandha bandhana kha khkha khādana hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2 svāhā. Having formed two vajra-fists joined back-to-back.

Enveloped by the earth-umbrella and lotus, [one should offer] a white *arocana* chain with the mantra: *Oṃ tiṣṭha 2 hūṃ bhakṣī 2 jaḥ phaṭ svāhā*. The southern *bali* offering should be given according to the stated characteristics. That place in the eastern direction [is prepared] with the eight common locations;
[it is marked] with twenty strokes and three *tālas*, resounded with the vajra and bell.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the offering and worship of the eight directions of the maṇḍala.
Then, for the disciple who has received the formal consent (*adhivāsana*), [the site] should be covered with a canopy toward the northeast and adorned with various hanging cloths;
and the seat, such as the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), should be decorated with various objects worthy of worship.

If a hero of wrath is available, or if not, then by means of those [visualized] ones through the application of Vajrasattva, one should place the disciple in front, adorned with all ornaments and standing with hands joined in the vajra-añjali gesture.

Having performed the ritual in its entirety, while the disciples are consuming the tooth-sticks and other items, one should recite *oṃ aḥ jihvā-saṃvartani hūṃ phaṭ* seven times over water and give it to all the disciples, saying: "Reciting this with care, may you cleanse your mouths in every way. May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, headed by Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnāgrya, Lokeśa, and Amoghasiddhi, attend to me—[I], named so-and-so, from this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment."
"I generate the supreme, unsurpassed bodhicitta,
just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment;
and I undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline and the gathering of wholesome qualities."
I firmly undertake the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings;
from this day forward, I shall observe the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha, taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels.
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality;
I shall also accept the master in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family,
and I shall bestow the four gifts six times every day.

I always accept the Dharma, material gifts, and the gift of fearlessness, as well as loving-kindness, within the Jewel Family; and the outer, secret, and three-vehicle teachings of the pure Great Lotus Family, which arises from great awakening.
I truly undertake the vow associated with all [the families],
performing acts of worship according to my ability within the exalted assembly of the great families of ritual action,
having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening.
I have undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings. I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are unliberated;
I shall bring comfort to those who are comfortless, and I shall establish sentient beings in nirvana. This is the glorious, supreme path that brings about the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
"By means of which you, when departing, shall become Tathāgatas. Having performed the consecration (*adhivāsana*) and honored [the deities] as prescribed, he should teach the Dharma;
having filled their minds, he should afterwards show them the entire mandala.

Then the preceptor, established in his own place and possessing the yoga of the nature of Vajrasattva, should again cause the song of the resonance of the vajra-bell to be sung: "O Harasirama! O you with the peaked crown! O you whose pair of feet are praised by jewels! O you who bear a body emerging from a throat constricted by a firm embrace!"
The pair of lotuses arising from the moving, quivering, and shifting secret [place] shines;
O Vajrasattva, Supreme Lord, the supreme state!
Thus ends the twentieth chapter: the ritual procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and the vows (*saṃvara*) of the disciple.
Then—
beginning with the rite of fire-oblation (homa) and so forth— one should satisfy all the deities to the east, north, or west of the maṇḍala.
Having carefully measured from the altar according to the sequence for pacification and nourishment,
