one should dig a square hole on the outside of the fourteenth *krānta* for the rite of pacification, and at the third [mark] of the non-*krānta*, two parts deep.
One should fashion the fourth part of that [measurement] as the lip itself;
and one-eighth of the lip shall be the eight-petaled lotus.
The outer wall of the lotus is one finger-width thick;
in the center of the sacrificial pit, vajras are placed upon the lotus.
CaPī II.1.9ab:

One should place the water of the five Buddhas marked with their respective symbols in each direction according to the directions. CaPī II.1.11cd: [One should place them] in each direction according to the directions.
In the four places of the lips, it is adorned with the mark of the Buddha;
one should cause the moon and vajra to be placed at each corner.
(CaPī II.1.12)
Just as the lofty and auspicious Kailāsa is [measured] by sites equal to thunderbolts,
so too is it joined with half a puruṣa and twelve aṅgulas.
One should establish the enclosure wall, the cage, and the stake in the eight directions of the site according to the sequence of the deities; all of these should be joined together as before.
One should imagine fire within that very mire of death and decay;
there, in the center, one should place a lotus adorned with the solar mandala.
Having drawn it forth by means of the syllable *ra* and the hook (*aṅkuśa*), the sensation [of heat] arises in the midst of the fire.
In accordance with the ritual procedures beginning with the offering of *argha* and *pādya*,
one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) smeared with the five products of the cow and milk,
along with curd, honey, milk, and cooked rice.
One should offer all grains, such as rice and other cereals, into the fire according to the prescribed ritual.
Having examined and considered all those [offerings], beginning with the pacification of the fire,
the wise practitioner should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth.
One should place a lotus in the center of the fire, and in its center, the Vajra-deity;
from the midst of all the deities who have dissolved therein, one should draw forth the goddess,
who resides in the center of the moon-maṇḍala and possesses a splendor like that of the full moon.
Having first honored all [the deities], the omniscient one should worship Vajrayoginī in the center with the essence of all reality (*sarvatattva*), together with the mudrās and mantras.
With the oblation of all substances, he should satisfy all the goddesses with: *oṃ sarvasaṃśodhani hūṃ phaṭ*.
The mantra for sprinkling the substances:
combined with the knowledge of the earth-umbrella and fashioned as a three-pronged vajra— OṂ HŪṂ AḤ SVĀHĀ.
With the oblation, one should offer the root-mantra and the fuel-sticks for the first; in the second, one should give ghee;
in the third, ghee mixed with honey and milk along with all types of grain; and in the fourth, the rite of offering is performed with milk-rice.
One should offer oblations of rice, ghee, and milk before the mandala,
one hundred and five times according to the reality; or, if possible, with more than that,
according to one's capacity, through this fire-offering one shall please all the deities.
Thereafter, having again combined [the offering] with an oblation of ghee for those who have mouths and tongues of sweetness,
and specifically by means of all the various oblations joined with the five nectars of ghee, one should prepare the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

One should perform the vajra song of the resonance of the vajra-bell: *Oṃ hūṃ 3*—O Vairocana, who teaches the yoga of selflessness as the nature of emanation and withdrawal, whose self is the state of equal yoga, homage be to you!
*Oṃ hūṃ 3*—the vision of the arising of the cause of the reality of emptiness and so forth.
O Knower of the Body of Knowledge, may there be no remainder for non-existence; having worshipped both externally and internally with all songs and dances,
the practitioner should once again offer the collection of the essence of the *piṇḍa* with the complete substances of the ritual, performing the yoga of the self.

Having offered five hundred oblations of *śrīphala* wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, along with fuel-sticks of the Bodhi tree and abundant *uḍyaka* flowers, one who is concentrated and intent on their vow should receive consecration in its midst.

O King of kings, for one who has fallen from his royal status, [one should offer] five hundred oblations of milk-mixed honey and abundant *samidh* wood with many offerings, using the *śrī* mantra; by this, he shall very swiftly become beautiful once again on earth.
Whatever intended action one contemplates, that will be accomplished in its entirety;
therefore, first, the wise practitioner should worship the Goddess in her own place within the yoga with various flowers and incense.

Having displayed all the applications of the heart-mudrā and mantra, they were all honored; then, with twenty vajra-bells, they performed a play. Having formed two vajra-fists joined back-to-back, the earth-canopy and lotus-enclosure were raised white with yellow orpiment.

Having thus stirred [the bell] with the mudrā, recite the mantra of the Vajra-bell mudrā: *oṃ vajraghaṇṭe hūṃ 3 hoḥ | oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇita praraṇite sarvabuddhapracālite | prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajradharahṛdayāvasaṃtoṣaṇi hūṃ 3 hoḥ 2 aḥ svāhā*. Having thus stirred it, [this is] the mantra of the Vajra-bell mudrā.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (*homa*) concerning the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Then: One should cause the five *ḍākinīs* to bestow [the offerings] together with the five hooks (*pañcāṅkuśa*) and so forth.

All those other hooks are, by virtue of the reality of the fifth hook, to be bestowed by all the *yoginīs*. The Knower of All, having firmly formed two fists encircled by knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*), [should perform this] both externally and internally.
Oṃ aḥ hūṃ hūṃ ghruṃ śruṃ svāhā.

This is the mantra of the five-hook mudrā (*pañcāṅkuśamudrā*). That which is produced solely from all flavors, [offered] by those in the south, west, and intermediate directions, is worshipped with vessels at the opening of the site, even in other locations.
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta) should be given to the well-discerning preceptor,
who is filled with great purity and the like;
having spread out the moon-hand (candrahasta), it is joined with the knowledge of the breaking [of the bonds].
One should fix a conch-shell at the top of the raised triple-bannered flag;
one should purify the five nectars through the reality of the previously mentioned mantras and so forth.
In the center of that, the syllables of nectar belonging to the Moon are shown: Oṃ haḥ ho hrīḥ śriṃ hūṃ aḥ svāhā.
The mantra for purifying the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) is as follows: "O Knower of the Distinctions! Churning is considered to be threefold;
one who knows the mantras of all yoginīs should repeatedly offer the *chiḍiṅga* [semen], filling vessels such as oyster shells, and should cause it to be given portion by portion."
The wise one should worship the one who is to be worshipped even by the Daityas according to the prescribed ritual;

furthermore, he should cause a song to be performed with the resonance of the vajra and the bell: "Hūṃ Hūṃ! O fierce Vajrasattva, you who are most excellent and have conquered passion, you who dwell in the heart of the wicked, do not abandon my body! O crusher of Māra and Madana, may my limbs not be destroyed! Hūṃ Hūṃ – Niṭṭhuru vajjusatta rāgāsahi uttamekkha piḍavisaï vasālu pāü mā bhejjaï aṅgu mahu mammatha mathaṇe khīṇu.

O Vajra, the most terrible destroyer of me alone; O Vettālī, O Caṇḍālī, who has cast me into the forest of saṃsāra—O Lord, deliver me! You are compassionate, you are the embodiment of mercy, you are the liberator.
O Liberation, you are the boat that carries one across the stream; having crushed and split apart my fourfold anger, [save me].
Behold, O King,
how he abandons his existence upon the drum; the Lord of Delusion, Rāvaṇa, who was the master of the five passions, has been crushed by you, O Lord of Men, whose feet are worshipped by the gods.
Purandara holds the parasol; Parjanya [holds] the fly-whisk;
Kamalāsana [holds] the chowrie; and Rati’s husband [holds] the vessel of betel-leaf.
Hari is his doorkeeper, and Hara utters his name.
"Go, go, Vajrasattva, you who have made the three worlds your own!

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the procedure for the emergence of all offerings beginning with the five hooks. Then—the worship of the heroes and so forth should be performed with a mind accompanied by the yoginīs;
having surrounded the eight directions, one should offer every seat.
With the yogas and yoginīs, in the single pair of seats,
O Yoginī of Reality, all those couples embrace one another’s breasts;
there is the erotic sentiment through the expression of laughter, resounded by vajras and bells.
One should offer all perfumes in succession, worship with all flowers, offer all incense, and cause all lamps to be given;
one should present every kind of sacrificial offering (bali) before the object of worship.
With hooks and various garments, without distinction, in five ways,
one should satisfy all the Yoginīs through the reality of the principle of Āditya;
the body consists of the essence of Yogāmbarī, as determined by the Ācārya.
I praise the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) within the conch, intent upon the ritual sprinkling;
having first uttered the mantra of the practitioner according to its true nature as previously stated, and having accepted it even while standing, one should afterwards give it to the Yoginī.
One should grasp [the teaching] through verse after verse from all aspects of the conduct of the *samaya*; having seen and purified the Dharma, one must not abandon its true nature (*sambhāva*).
A Brahmin, a dog, and a *caṇḍāla*—these are all consumed within the single nature [of reality].
(CaPī II.3.133) Others should likewise grasp it, preceded by the *kamalāvartana* [mudrā].
One who is skilled in the analysis [of the text] should join the remainder with the raised needle;
having established the sun and the moon, one should recite these verses for him: "Welcome is the Dharma, priceless, stainless, unattainable, avoiding the grasp of grasping; bow down with devotion."

CaPī II.3.136. Now, in the sequence [of the phonemes], when all [the vowels] are joined with *su* in the sense of "all," for all those yogins who have attained mastery through their own will, while singing the auspicious song (*maṅgalāgīti*),
the *alikāli* (the union of vowels and consonants) of the heroes arises as completely pure.

One should sing the song of reality (*tattvagīta*) to the resonance of the vajra-bell: "O you who are free from the suffering of worldly existence, you who bestow liberation; you who dwell in the terrible forest of passion, you who delight in the circle of passion (*ratimaṇḍala*);

you who have abandoned the distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, you who rest in the void; O terrifying one, cause the world to be liberated! Having worshipped with various auspicious offerings through the vajra-song, [one honors] the remnant of the hero's desire through the resonance of the vajra-bell."

Filling the mouth, one whose mind is focused solely on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) should cast [the offering] while contemplating whatever rite is to be performed upon the vessel for the *bali*: *Oṃ kuru 2 vattali mahāvattali śiddhimukhe śmaśānavāsinī pretamukhi caṇḍakarāli rudhirapriye pretasamayarakṣitayogadharī kilikilirāve pitṛvanamadhye bhuñjaha bhakṣaha grahagaṇabhūte dhūmāṅgāricaṇḍakarāli tiṣṭha svīkuru 2 hūṃ gṛhṇa 2 sarvaduṣṭān bhakṣa 2 ho 2 phruṃ pheṃ phaṭ svāhā.*
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should raise the white *arocana* [pigment] and, with the two tips bent, place it on the sides of the mouth.

This is the mudrā and mantra for the remains of the offering (*ucchiṣṭa-bali*), the smoke, and the charcoal. [It is to be used] at a crossroads, in a cemetery, on a mountain, at a tree, or by a great river.
The dismissal with three snaps of the fingers while holding the five offerings in the hands and so forth;

thus ends the twenty-third chapter on the ritual for all worship and the offering of the discarded *bali*. Then: Having filled a conch shell with the ten substances mixed with fragrant milk, one should sprinkle the vessel with the *samaya* water. Reciting "Oṃ aḥ hūṃ aḥ svāhā" seven times, one should consecrate it as the *samaya* water.
There, one should initiate each disciple individually;
having led them in with their eyes covered by cloth, they should be made to join their palms in añjali before the preceptor, who holds a handful of flowers in his own joined palms.

Today, the disciple should first generate the bodhicitta of aspiration for the supreme saṃsāra, and then perform the meditation on the emptiness of intrinsic nature and so forth: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*;
*oṃ vajraśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ vajraśuddho ’ham*.

Having performed the threefold purification by saying, "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga," one should speak thus: "I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the Three Jewels. O Vajra, be my protection from fear everywhere; I am one who desires that which is free from fear. I am a possessor of the essential substance.
For one who possesses loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth, and is protected by the restraint of ethical discipline: *Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the worshipful five ḍākinīs;
Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the worshipful master;
Oṃ, I offer myself for the sake of protecting all sentient beings.*

*Samayas tvam samayas tvam ho 2.* The letter *A*, the foremost of all letters, is empowered as the Vajra of Speech (*vāgvajra*). The letter *I*, the form of desire, is empowered as the Vajra of Body (*kāyavajra*) in the heart.

The syllable *Hūṃ*, which burns away the afflictions (*kleśa*), is empowered as the Vajra in the heart. *Oṃ hili 2 maṇa ghūrṇṇita vajrācale yuṃ 3 hūṃ svāhā.* I am the primordial wisdom among the wise; make [this] the taste of nectar (*amṛta*).

Oṃ durgatyāpahara aḥ svāhā. With this mantra, one should cause [the five nectars] to be offered into the mouth of the conch. Then, having prepared the disciple, the descent [of the deity] should be performed. One should place the deity within the heart; in the center of the wind-enclosure is the seed-syllable of wind (yaṃ).
Wind upon wind is at the feet, and the blazing wind is in the heart.

One should [visualize] the Wisdom-Ḍākinī as oneself, resounding with the fierce sound of the syllable *hūṃ*. With the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) of the resonance of the Vajra-bell—*oṃ aḥ le 3 hūṃ aḥ*—the yogins should sing the Vajra-song. Dancing most fiercely, they should dance according to their own will; one should always cause them to act according to their own will. *Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra samaya pratipālaka hūṃ 3 ho 3 svāhā.*

The mantra for dismissal (*visarjana-mantra*): Then, having cast a flower in its proper place, one should recognize the distinction between the families of the deities and bestow the mantras, mudrās, and so forth. *Oṃ jñānacakṣu hūṃ aḥ svāhā*. Having thus opened his eyes and paid homage, the reality (*tattva*) of the deity is revealed—the God who is the sovereign of all, the omniscient one dwelling in the abode of the thirty-three gods, the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Jñāna-Ḍākinī, marked by the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To the east is Vajraḍākinī, seated upon a serpent crown, known by the name Yogāmbarī; she is stainless with pure knowledge, arisen from wisdom, and the crusher of all that is evil.
Arising from the single source of all flavors, equal toward all sentient beings,
the burner of all enemies of Māra, the Terrible One— may she look upon the stainlessness of the investigation into the ten unwholesome actions and so forth. A 25v.
Behold Vettālī in the west, seated upon the Garuḍa throne;
she is born from all ritual limbs and is the subduer of Hari and Hara.
Behold Caṇḍālī in the south, the burner of all afflictions.
From the womb-cavity of a lioness, a tigress, and an owl came a female jackal;
seated upon the throne of a lioness, she was a female jackal who,
through various forms and great skillful means, acted for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The Ḍākinī, Dīpinī, Cūṣikā, Kāmbojī, and Dvārapālinī;
Akarṣiṇī, Bandhanī, Sphoṭanī, and Toṣaṇī;
Pokkasī, Drāmiḍī, Caṇḍī, and Saubhāgī—all these goddesses stand with hands busy with offerings.
Ghorī, with her hands busily occupied holding vessels of lotuses filled with five-fold goads of blood and flesh;
Ugrī, blazing and loathsome, with hands deeply sunk in the mud of the sacrificial offering.
Kapālī, Vajrī, and Kumbhīnā, with their hands busily occupied with lotuses according to the prescribed methods of eating and holding;
Lāsyā with perfumes and the like; and Dhūpikā with flowers and song for the lute-player.
Beginning with the dancing lamps and so forth, one should worship all directions and sub-directions; thereafter,
one should worship Brahmā in the form of the doorkeeper and holding a fly-whisk for Hari,
and Śakra as the umbrella-bearer for Rudra, while proclaiming their names.
While he was blocking the gates of the sacrifice with his own forces accompanied by swans,
King Varuṇa approached from the northeast corner with his army and his wife, who was preoccupied with various offerings.
In the *Vimāravarapūra*, everything has been declared by the Deity as characterized by reality;

thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the Ritual for the Worship of the Deity. Then, having performed obeisance with the five limbs, one should specifically offer water for the hands (*argha*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), and entreat [the deity]: "O Great-Souled One, grant your grace according to my own desired dharma."
"Grant it! Cause it to be granted! I shall entreat for the state of the Vajrayogāmbarī;
I shall become irreversible through the hosts of Vajrayoginīs.
Then, the disciple should be made to form a hollowed cup with joined palms.
Oṃ, I have entered the great maṇḍala of the vajra-maṇḍala;
Oṃ, I have been shown the great maṇḍala of the yoga-maṇḍala;
Oṃ, I have been initiated into the great maṇḍala of the secret maṇḍala.

"Samaya! You are the pledge, ho! ho! The disciple should be known from the perspective of ultimate reality as the Lion of Orators (Vādisiṃha). For the purpose of cutting through the cloth-band of the designation of yoga, may the faults of existence and the afflictions be struck down;
may they be sprinkled with the supreme king of the true reality of the ultimate yoga. Thus, the vajra-fist is joined with the sun by means of the knowledge of the conch.
Having fashioned oneself as the deity through the eight limbs of the ritual, one should place the syllable *kṣūṃ* on the crown of the head, *huṃ* on the two eyes,
*yuṃ* between the ears and nose, and the brilliantly blazing *suṃ* on the tongue.

One should assign *smryūṃ* to the neck, *kūṭa* to the chest, *ymryūṃ* to the region of the heart, and *hmryūṃ* to the navel; thus, in this sequence, one performs the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpana*), which is maintained by the seed-syllables of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅgabīja*) along with the mudrās.
Then: *Oṃ samayo ’ham* (I am the pledge), *oṃ*.
Oṃ, I am the Vajra—Āḥ! Oṃ, I am Gnosis—Hūṃ! Oṃ, I am the Turner—Ho! 26vḥ.
Oṃ, I am Udbhava! A ĀṂ HŪṂ SVĀHĀ. One should recite this while holding the body of gnosis (jñānakāya) of reality.
Then, the secret instruction should be given, and one should cause him to receive the empowerment.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for the armor-instruction of the eight yoginīs. Thereafter, the empowerment should be given from the south, west, and north.
The eastern gate was [consecrated] by the master with a water-pot;
the lion throne, adorned with a parasol above the heads of the first five [deities],
was occupied by one seated on a *bhadrāsana* with hands joined in the *saṃpuṭāñjali* gesture.
With a mind of bodhicitta, one should visualize the supreme Praṇidhisattva, resounding with the sound of auspicious songs and the ringing of vajra-bells,
facing east and so forth, while the Ācārya stands to the west.
Through the yoga of Vajrasattva and the others, the flask is like the sun and moon;
with the vase of the water of gnosis, marked by a vajra and adorned with sprouts,
may there be the empowerment of perfect awakening today, crossing over from saṃsāra— oṃ aḥ phraṃ phreṃ phaṭ hūṃ svāhā.

The initiation mantra is: *Oṃ vajrakāya hūṃ āḥ svāhā*. With the *vajrasphoṭika* mudrā, one should perform the binding of protection for the eight locations using white *arocana* and a chain. One should place a sun-vajra upon the sun [disk] and a bell upon the moon.
On the head, the five Buddhas are joined with the mudrā-mantra.
Having formed two *vajramuṣṭi* fists, one raises the white *arocana*.

Kissing the smoke-stained impurity raised at the tip [of the tongue], *oṃ hūṃ āḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the consecration of the five Buddhas by the mudrā of the *Ghaṭa* (Vase). The state of universal sovereignty should be bestowed; indeed, the *Nāmavajra* (Name-Vajra) is given with the hands. The *Vajravratā* (Vow-Vajra), however, consists of dance and so forth, according to rule and in proper sequence.
In that regard, these mantras and mudrās shall be the determination for all the Buddhas:
"Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the consecration of the Yogāmbarīs."

"Take this, which is the state of all Buddhas, O Vajra, for the sake of perfect accomplishment! Oṃ! I consecrate you as Śrī Yogāmbarī; remain, O Hero! You are the Samaya, the being without beginning or end, Vajrasattva, the Great Joy, Samantabhadra, the soul of all, Lord of the Vajra-Arrogance, Lord! This is the Vajra; she is remembered as the one who follows the sound of wisdom among all the Yoginīs.
It must indeed always be held by you, for supreme enlightenment is considered the goal by the Victors."
Existence is indeed pure by nature, yet it is made non-existent by natures that are themselves devoid of existence;

through beings who are truly pure by nature, supreme existence is brought about. Embracing the bell with the vajra-bell, holding the left cheek with pride, one should consecrate the Mahāmudrā, whose essence is the yoga of the non-dual duality.

Now, for the empowerment of sovereignty (*adhipatyābhiṣeka*), one who possesses the yoga of the self-nature of all Buddhas should bestow the *ālikāli* by means of the seed-syllable upon the recipient of the mantra-empowerment. "O Śrī Yogāmbarī, I empower you through the name-empowerment (*nāmābhiṣeka*). By means of the name beginning with the word "Śrī," this is the name-empowerment. This is that state of all-buddhahood which abides within the sphere of the secret vajra.

For you too must always firmly maintain the vow of the *yogāmbara*. Oṃ, O Vajra-samaya accomplished by all Tathāgatas, remain! I maintain you now—Hūṃ Hrīḥ. From this moment forth, together with the Perfect Buddhas, the Yoginīs, and their sons, through the great pride of wisdom and means, and with the festivals of blissful dance-offerings, the Yoginī of all Heroes should dance gracefully and strike with the garland. "Become the primordial yoga"—with these words, the garland is indeed their ornament. Sing the song of all the True Dharma for all embodied beings.

Then, O practitioner of excellent vows, having offered fragrance and incense to the Yoginīs, place the Buddhist wick within them; through the scent, incense, and the offering of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*), you shall quickly experience union with ease.
By means of the knowledge of the Sugata’s possession within embodied beings, you shall gladden the Yoginīs; like Vajradharma himself, you shall illuminate the lamp of the Dharma.

Illuminate with the light of wisdom those beings blinded by ignorance; O child, remove the veil of nescience from them, just as the Jinas— those sovereign physicians of the world— removed the cataracts of the eye from the people.
Oṃ! O Vajranetrā, remove the film! Hrīḥ! These phenomena are like reflections in a mirror; they are transparent, pure, and unclouded.
They are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from causes and karma.
Knowing these phenomena to be thus, their nature is without abode.

Perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings; you have been born upon the breast of Yoga-nī as a mirror for the sake of the welfare of all beings. In all worlds and at all times, set in motion the wheel of Dharma—the universal way of conduct and practice. You have neither doubt nor hesitation; with a mind free from uncertainty, [turn the wheel].
The supreme Dharma-conch, stainless and possessing all perfections, is held by the ear of the upper garment on the left; it is the conch that grants fearlessness and reassurance with the right hand,
while one’s own self is Jñānaḍākinī, established within all the cakras.
With one voice, they all proclaimed the entire *Yogāmbarī-vyākaraṇa* as follows:

“I hereby prophesy you, having raised you from the miserable states of existence, for the sake of ultimate purification from cyclic existence: you are the Tathāgatī named Śrī Yogāmbarī; this is the accomplishment and the pledge (*samaya*). Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! You have emerged!”

Having embraced the Perfection of Wisdom itself, one should intensely visualize the seed-syllable consisting of the five Buddhas as a play of flowers within the interior of the blossom; one should not place there that which is fashioned from the three groups of three.
Thus honored by the heroes who are skilled in overcoming opposing factors and by the Great Auspiciousness that is like Mount Sumeru,
the Hero who possesses the yoga of the self-nature of all Buddhas should reveal the first syllable of each [mantra] as the five Buddhas and so forth.
One should cause [the disciple] to meditate on the eight syllables conjoined with the mantra-consecration;
however, for the master-consecration, one should reveal knowledge and realization;
and for one joined with the yoga-consecration, all the secrets and so forth are explained.
All this is the supreme state of the great secret empowerment; it is for one who is previously established in the Dharma, and not for one who would cause harm to sentient beings or the like.
For one intent on harshness, even after disparaging [the teaching], one should always remain in happiness.
May they observe the vow of ethical discipline, practicing non-violence toward all living beings;
for one who harms living creatures, even meeting death is better than that.
One should not touch the wealth and possessions of others, nor the fires of others, as if they were blazing fires.
For yogis who are protected from falsehood by means of subtle and other such practices,
there is no falsehood in their practice of yoga;
even while practicing self-restraint, they remain within that restraint through their conduct regarding food and drink.

In self-restraint there is the play of delight; by means of self-restraint and through the power of the time [of practice], yogins who desire accomplishment succeed once they have propitiated the *sattva*. Therefore, one should demonstrate to the disciple an *asarvajña* (non-omniscient) *sattva* that inspires enthusiasm.
Having accomplished the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), it is shown that one is equal to all; through the yoga and meditation of constant conduct, and being intent upon that,
having first undertaken the training, one is empowered within the mandalas.
O Child, having observed the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings,
I shall live for one [day] according to your command, O Lord, just as it was known by you, the foremost disciple and predecessor, in accordance with reality, whether in sequence or non-sequence.

One should cause the Daityas and others to worship [the deity] and make them bow down to the gods; one should demonstrate this to all sentient beings through the essential principles for all disciples and so forth.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Procedure for the Instruction on All Consecrations.
Then— the disciple who possesses the realization that his entire self belongs to the Guru must give the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*);
whether it be his wife along with his sons, his kinsmen, male and female servants,
his territories, his house and field, his clothes, or even his own body, he should offer it for the sake of liberation.

One should prepare as a teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā) silver, copper, and other metals; various grains of all kinds of rice; a seat, an umbrella, sandals, a bed with its furnishings, and even one's own body.
If a disciple is lacking in devotion, there will undoubtedly be suffering and affliction.

With every aspect of his being, the disciple must first offer the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā); he should worship all the [deities] beginning with the first, using the mudrās for incense, perfumes, flowers, and so forth.

In the form of auspicious songs, resounding with the vajra and bell: *Hūṃ* 3 — O Protector, you are liberation; you are the one who teaches the Dharma; you are the cause, the non-cause, the existent, the non-existent, and liberation. O Liberation, you are the manifestation and the dissolution of phenomena; O God, you are the liberation of reality.

One should perform an offering consisting of auspicious songs, hymns, and praises, saying: "Do not strike my lord! Alas, O Vajra, you [have struck him]! Alas, O Mokṣa, you! Then: *oṃ rama 2 ho hī 3 hūṃ hoḥ aḥ;
oṃ rama 2 hoḥ 2 hūṃ 2 hoḥ he aḥ;
oṃ rama 2 phruṃ phraṃ phreṃ phroṃ aḥ*.

Oṃ rama 2 hoḥ ghu 2 ghrāṃ gho aḥ svāhā. This is the mālā-mantra of the eight ḍākinīs. Having satisfied the sun and moon, having formed a hollowed cup of flowers with joined palms (añjali), and having made a prayer for the sake of all sentient beings, one should generate the great mind (mahācitta).
"I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall liberate those who are not liberated.
While this is being recited, O King of kings, one should cause the disciple to offer [the gift] as prescribed in all the previous [traditions] according to the practice of the Yogaśāstra.

All the lords of the giving of gifts, with palms joined in reverence, having consecrated the flowers and so forth from the water of the conch as it remains in every state, should diligently cause them to be given [to the disciple], saying:
"You are liberated from the ocean of existence in saṃsāra; you are Vajrasattva, born from Vajrasattva."

"For one who has been consecrated with the crown of a Perfect Buddha, for the sake of sentient beings, and for one whose intention is swift"—having spoken thus, [the ritual] should be performed according to the procedure for dismissal.
This is the twenty-seventh chapter: the Ritual for the Teacher’s Fee, the Disciple’s Apology, and Worship.

Then, having firmly formed the vajra-añjali mudrā, those who have compassion for all sentient beings—knowing the mantra of the threefold pride of the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind—should recite: *Oṃ namo ’stu hūṃ namāmi hūṃ namo namaḥ hūṃ svāhā*.
Having formed two vajra-fists, they should press them against the moon at the heart.

Having established [the deity] on the solar ground, the mantra is firmly recited: *Oṃ alo tiṣṭha svāhā*. Entering the heart of the wisdom-maṇḍala: *Oṃ gaccha 2 svabhavanaṃ hūṃ svāhā*. Dismissing the commitment-wheel (*samayacakra*): *Oṃ gaccha 2 punar āgamanāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. One should perform three snaps of the fingers for the dismissal of the worldly deities: *Oṃ ghili 2 nadyā hūṃ jaḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the removal of the colored powders (*rajasaṃhāra*); one should diligently cause the powders to flow away into a great river.

Having set aside the remnants of the *bali* offering, one should give them at a crossroads or by a river with the mantra for reciting over the remaining *bali*: *oṃ hili 2 phuṃ li mahā phuṃ li phe phe svāhā*. One should again perform the worship and other rites, including the drinking of water and the offering of food.
In that place, however, one should prepare a yellow powder and so forth, forming an eight-petaled lotus adorned with filaments and a pericarp.
Accompanied by the Daityas and Bali, following the sequence of mantras and mudrās,
one should perform the entire grand worship of the secret wheel-manifestation,
together with the disciples, using mantras, auspicious songs, and dances.
From Yogāmbarī comes Buddha; from her, the Lord Vairocana.
From Vajraḍākinī comes Ārya Māmakī;
from Ghorāḍākinī comes Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
From where there is Vetālāḍākinī, from there is Āryatārā;
and from where there is Caṇḍālāḍākinī, from there is Buddhalocanā; Siddhadūtī is the fourfold miraculous transformation of the entire body.
The merit of giving increases according to the distinction between a pure field and other fields:
one thousand Śūdras are equal to one pure Brāhmaṇa; indeed, one thousand Brāhmaṇas are equal to one Bhikṣu. One should employ [the gift] toward a single Bhikṣu.
One thousand and two hundred monks are equal to one particle of dust;
one hundred thousand particles of dust are equal to one wise man; one thousand and two hundred wise men are indeed considered equal to one teacher.
Thus, why would one not give a gift to a field that is an excellent field?
Since the roots of Dharma are based on renunciation, one should sow the seed in an excellent field;
by doing so, one will be liberated from even the dust of the sins of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).
Having entered into the reality of mantra, one is reborn in the Pure Abodes;
for those skilled in the arts, this sequence of awakening quickly bestows the gift [of realization].
Her form blazes throughout the three worlds, and she is disciplined by Anurāgaṇa.
Pervaded by thousands of rays, possessing the brilliance of ten thousand suns,
and abounding in various delights,
pleasures, and virtues, the supreme lord Yogāmbara dances with playful gait.
One should please Vajrayoginī with the syllable *hūṃ* as a song;
being well-composed, one should sing with auspicious and sweet melodies.
[The mandala] consists of twelve thousand [verses] in brief, but the four seats (*catuḥpīṭha*) are extensive.
Its points of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are a compendium of the essential core; the meaning of the words of desire and reasoning is not a synthesis with [ordinary] meaning,
but is spoken in the Mleccha language, concealed by the reality of yoga (*yogatattva*).
Thus ends the twenty-seventh [chapter], the Ritual Manual for the Mandala, detailing the extensive procedure for the worship of all yogic dances and songs, in the *Catuṣpīṭha-mahāyoginī-tantrarāja*.
This is the manual for the mandala ritual composed by Caryāvrati Pādāḥ.
